Forgetting the rn alias in the CTE rewrite must be referenced by name in the outer WHERE clause
keyPoints: QUALIFY filters on a window function's result after it has been computed, which WHERE cannot do
QUALIFY plays the same logical role for window functions that HAVING plays for aggregates
QUALIFY improves readability by keeping ranking and filtering logic in one statement
QUALIFY is a Snowflake-originated extension adopted by some platforms, not universal ANSI SQL
Migrating off QUALIFY requires only a mechanical CTE-plus-WHERE rewrite; the window function logic is unchanged

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides correct QUALIFY query and correct CTE rewrite for non-supporting platforms
Correctly explains what QUALIFY does and why WHERE cannot achieve the same thing
Correctly identifies which platforms support/don't support QUALIFY
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Writing Unity Catalog Row Filters and Column Masks for a Shared Customer Table
questions.prompt: A single gold.customers table in Unity Catalog needs to be shared across sales, support, and finance, but sales reps must only see rows for their own assigned region, and nobody outside finance should see the raw SSN column (everyone else should see it masked). Write the Unity Catalog DDL that implements both a row-level filter and a column mask, and explain how these differ mechanically from building three separate views.
questions.code:
CREATE FUNCTION governance.region_row_filter(region STRING)
RETURN
  IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('finance_team')
  OR region = (SELECT assigned_region FROM governance.sales_assignments WHERE user_name = current_user());

ALTER TABLE gold.customers
SET ROW FILTER governance.region_row_filter ON (region);

CREATE FUNCTION governance.ssn_mask(ssn STRING)
RETURN
  CASE WHEN IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('finance_team')
       THEN ssn
       ELSE CONCAT('***-**-', RIGHT(ssn, 4))
  END;

ALTER TABLE gold.customers
ALTER COLUMN ssn SET MASK governance.ssn_mask;
questions.modelAnswer:
A row filter is a SQL function registered against the table that's evaluated for every row at query time, and its boolean result determines whether that row is visible to the querying user -- here, IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('finance_team') grants finance an unconditional pass, while everyone else's visibility is determined by comparing the row's region column against whatever region is on file for current_user() in a sales_assignments lookup table. A column mask works the same mechanical way but transforms a column's value instead of filtering rows: the ssn_mask function returns the real SSN unmasked for finance and a redacted version (keeping only the last four digits) for everyone else, evaluated per row per query just like the row filter.

The critical mechanical difference from building three separate views is where the policy lives and how many places it has to be kept correct. Three views means three separate SELECT statements, each independently encoding its own version of 'who should see what,' and every one of those views sits on top of the same underlying table -- which means any new consumer (a new BI tool, a new ad hoc query, a new pipeline) has to know to query the correct view for their role rather than the base table, and nothing stops someone from just querying gold.customers directly and bypassing all three views' logic entirely. Row filters and column masks are attached directly to the base table object itself in Unity Catalog's metadata, so there is no 'unprotected' path to the data -- any query against gold.customers, from any tool, by any user, through any future integration, automatically has the row filter and column mask applied, because the policy is enforced at the table, not reimplemented per consumer.

This also means a single policy change -- adding a new region, changing who counts as finance, adjusting the masking format -- is a change to one function definition, not a hunt through every view, every BI tool's semantic layer, and every ad hoc script that might have independently encoded the same business rule. That centralization is exactly the governance property Unity Catalog's three-level namespace and attached policies are designed to provide: one place to audit, one place to change, and a guarantee that enforcement travels with the table rather than depending on every future consumer remembering to use the 'right' derived object.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A row filter is just a function attached to the table that runs per row and returns true or false for whether the current user gets to see that row -- here finance gets an automatic pass, and everyone else only sees rows matching whatever region is on file for them in a lookup table. A column mask works the same way mechanically but transforms a value instead of hiding a row -- finance sees the real SSN, everyone else sees a redacted version, decided by the same per-row, per-query evaluation.

The reason I'd do this instead of three separate views comes down to where the enforcement actually lives. Three views means three separate places independently encoding 'who sees what,' sitting on top of the same base table -- and nothing stops a new tool, a new pipeline, or someone writing an ad hoc query from just querying gold.customers directly and skipping all three views' logic entirely. Attaching the row filter and column mask straight to the table itself in Unity Catalog means there's no unprotected path -- every single query against that table, from any tool, by anyone, automatically gets the filter and mask applied, because the enforcement travels with the table object, not with whichever derived view someone happened to remember to use.

It also means when the policy needs to change -- a new region gets added, finance's membership changes, we want a different masking format -- that's a change to one function, not a search-and-replace across three views and however many BI tools' own semantic layers might have quietly reimplemented the same rule. That's really the whole value proposition here: one place to audit, one place to change, and a guarantee it's actually enforced everywhere rather than hoped for everywhere.
commonMistakes: Building separate views per role instead of attaching governance directly to the base table
Assuming a view-based approach is equally secure as long as 'everyone knows' to use the right view
Forgetting row filters and column masks are evaluated per query, so the underlying lookup tables they reference must stay performant
Not testing the row filter/mask behavior for a user who belongs to no mapped region, leaving an unhandled edge case
Granting broad SELECT on the base table that bypasses the intended audience without verifying the filter/mask actually applies to every grant path
keyPoints: Row filters and column masks are functions attached directly to the table, evaluated per row per query
They differ from views by closing off any unprotected path to the base table, not just adding a derived layer
A single function change updates policy everywhere the table is queried, from any tool
This centralizes both the audit surface and the maintenance burden compared to per-consumer views
Edge cases (e.g., a user with no assigned region) must be explicitly handled in the row filter logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides correct DDL for a row filter and a column mask
Correctly explains the per-row, per-query evaluation mechanism
Correctly explains why this differs from and improves on a view-based approach
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Power BI Report That Got Slow After It Grew Past 50,000 Views
questions.prompt: A Power BI report that used to load in two seconds now takes twenty seconds, and the only thing that changed is organic growth: the underlying import-mode semantic model has grown from 5 million to 60 million rows, and the report added a few more visuals on the same page. You open Performance Analyzer. Walk through exactly what you look for to tell whether this is a visual rendering problem, a DAX query problem, or a VertiPaq storage engine problem, and what you'd actually fix for each case.
questions.modelAnswer:
Performance Analyzer breaks every visual's load time into three buckets, and reading those buckets correctly is the whole diagnosis: DAX query time (how long the query engine took to produce the result set, split further into Formula Engine and Storage Engine time if you dig into the underlying query via 'Copy query'), Visual display time (actually rendering the visual once data is back), and Other (everything else, often cross-visual/cross-filter overhead). A problem that's purely about rendering shows up as a long Visual display time with a short DAX query time -- that points at the visual itself: too many data points for the visual type to render efficiently (a huge scatter plot or a table with thousands of visible rows), too many visuals on one page competing for rendering at once, or custom/overly complex conditional formatting and visual-level filtering applied per-element.

If instead the DAX query time dominates, you need to split it further between Formula Engine (FE) and Storage Engine (SE) time -- Performance Analyzer's 'Copy query' button lets you run the actual query in DAX Studio, which breaks this down precisely. A high SE time relative to FE usually means VertiPaq itself is scanning more data than it needs to for the result -- which is extremely plausible here given the model grew 12x in row count, especially if a measure's filter logic doesn't prune effectively (a non-SARGable-equivalent pattern in DAX, like filtering on a calculated column that can't be pushed down, or an iterator scanning the full fact table because a relationship isn't set up to let the engine prune early). A high FE time relative to SE, on the other hand, points at the query itself doing expensive row-by-row context-transition-heavy work in the formula engine -- single-threaded by design -- which is a classic symptom of iterator-heavy or nested-CALCULATE-heavy measures that don't parallelize no matter how fast storage engine scans are.

The fixes split cleanly along this diagnosis. For a pure rendering problem: reduce the data density per visual (apply TOPN, aggregate before visualizing, or add a 'too many data points' drill-down pattern instead of rendering everything at once), and reduce the number of simultaneously-rendering visuals on one page. For a storage-engine-dominated DAX problem at this new scale: this is exactly where aggregations become valuable -- building a pre-aggregated table at a coarser grain that VertiPaq can serve from directly for anything that doesn't need row-level detail, and letting the engine's automatic aggregation-hit-detection route eligible queries there instead of scanning the full 60-million-row fact table every time; incremental refresh policies also become worth implementing at this scale if refresh time (a related but separate problem) is also growing. For a formula-engine-dominated problem: the fix is almost always rewriting the measure itself -- replacing iterator patterns that trigger unnecessary context transition with SUMX/CALCULATE patterns that let more work happen in the storage engine, which parallelizes, instead of the formula engine, which doesn't.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is always Performance Analyzer's breakdown by visual, because it already splits the time into DAX query, Visual display, and Other, and that split alone usually tells you which of the three buckets you're actually in before you've written a single line of diagnostic DAX.

If Visual display time is the big number and DAX query time is small, it's a rendering problem, not a data problem -- too many data points for that visual type, too many visuals competing for the page, or heavy conditional formatting. The fix there is usually just reducing what's being rendered -- aggregate before plotting, cap the row count, cut the number of visuals sharing a page.

If DAX query time is the big number, I go pull that exact query into DAX Studio with the Copy Query button, specifically to split Formula Engine time from Storage Engine time, because they point at completely different fixes. High Storage Engine time usually means VertiPaq is scanning way more of the now-60-million-row fact table than it needs to -- that's the classic case for building an aggregation table at a coarser grain so most queries never touch the full fact table at all. High Formula Engine time points somewhere else entirely -- it means the measure itself is doing expensive row-by-row work, often an iterator triggering context transition unnecessarily, and formula engine work is single-threaded, so no amount of hardware fixes that -- you have to actually rewrite the measure to push more of the work into the storage engine instead.

So the short version: Performance Analyzer tells you which of three buckets you're in, DAX Studio's FE/SE split tells you which half of the DAX bucket is the problem if that's where you landed, and the fix is either visual-density reduction, an aggregation table, or a measure rewrite -- and I wouldn't guess at which one without actually looking.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to rewriting DAX measures without first checking whether the bottleneck is actually visual rendering
Not splitting DAX query time into Formula Engine vs Storage Engine time before deciding on a fix
Assuming more hardware/bigger capacity fixes a Formula Engine bottleneck, which is single-threaded regardless
Building an aggregation table before confirming Storage Engine scan time is actually the dominant cost
Treating 'the model grew' as an unfixable fact rather than an aggregation-table opportunity
keyPoints: Performance Analyzer splits visual load time into DAX query, Visual display, and Other
A rendering-dominated problem points at visual density/complexity, not the data model
DAX Studio's FE/SE split further diagnoses a DAX-query-dominated problem
High Storage Engine time suggests an aggregation table is needed at the new data scale
High Formula Engine time suggests a measure rewrite is needed since FE work doesn't parallelize

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes Performance Analyzer's three-way time breakdown
Correctly explains the Formula Engine vs Storage Engine distinction and diagnosis
Proposes correct, distinct fixes for each diagnosis category
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Tableau Dashboard That Times Out Only for Certain Users
questions.prompt: A Tableau Cloud dashboard built on a live custom SQL connection runs fine for most users but times out for users in the EMEA sales filter segment specifically. The custom SQL joins four tables and applies a WHERE clause that references a Tableau parameter. Walk through your diagnostic approach and what you'd actually change, including whether you'd move off custom SQL and what extract strategy you'd consider instead.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing to check is whether custom SQL is being treated as an opaque, un-optimizable block by Tableau's own query generation -- which it is, structurally. A live connection built on custom SQL gets wrapped by Tableau in an outer query (effectively SELECT * FROM (your custom SQL) WHERE ... for whatever filters and parameters the dashboard adds), which means the four-table join and its predicates execute first as their own subquery before any Tableau-level filtering -- including the EMEA segment filter, if it's applied as a Tableau filter rather than inside the custom SQL itself -- ever gets a chance to push down and reduce the join's input size. If EMEA happens to be the largest or least selective segment in the underlying data (more sales reps, more transaction volume, or a join that fans out worse for that region specifically), that segment's users are the ones who feel this the most sharply, because the full four-table join runs at full size for every single query before any segment-specific reduction happens, and the live database connection has to re-execute that join from scratch on every interaction.

Diagnosing this concretely means getting the actual generated SQL Tableau is sending to the database -- via the Performance Recording dashboard (built into Tableau, logs query execution time per event) or the database's own query log -- and checking whether the EMEA-filtered query is doing a full join-then-filter versus whatever a hand-written, filter-pushed-down equivalent query would do; if the custom SQL's WHERE clause doesn't already include the parameter/filter logic in a way the database's optimizer can use early (e.g., it's applied in Tableau's outer wrapper rather than inside the custom SQL), that's the smoking gun. It's also worth checking whether EMEA specifically triggers a worse join plan on the underlying database due to data skew or a missing/stale index on the join or filter columns for that segment's rows, which custom SQL makes harder to tune because Tableau isn't generating a straightforward queryable form the database's optimizer has an easy time with.

The real fix is almost always to move off a live custom SQL connection for this use case. Custom SQL blocks Tableau's own query optimization and makes the join opaque to both Tableau and, often, the database's optimizer in ways a native multi-table join configured directly in Tableau's data source (with proper join types and, if needed, join calculations) would not. Beyond that, for a live connection carrying this much join and filter complexity, switching to an extract is usually the higher-leverage move: an extract pre-materializes the join once, on a schedule, into Tableau's own fast columnar engine (Hyper), so every subsequent user interaction -- including filtering to EMEA -- queries the already-joined, already-optimized extract rather than re-running a four-table join live against the source database on every click. If genuinely live, second-by-second freshness is a real requirement (which is worth confirming rather than assuming), the fallback is to replace the custom SQL with native joins plus pushing the EMEA-equivalent filtering logic as early as possible, and to work with the DBA to ensure the join and filter columns are properly indexed specifically for the EMEA data pattern that's triggering the timeout.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first suspicion with any live custom SQL connection is that Tableau treats it as a black box -- it wraps your custom SQL in an outer query for its own filters and parameters, which means the whole four-table join runs first, at full size, before any Tableau-level filter including the EMEA segment filter gets a chance to reduce it. If EMEA happens to be the biggest or messiest segment in the underlying data, that's exactly the group that's going to feel a full unreduced join the hardest, every single time they interact with the dashboard.

To confirm it, I'd turn on Tableau's Performance Recording and look at the actual generated SQL and its execution time for an EMEA session versus a non-EMEA session, or just pull it from the database's own query log. I'm looking for whether the EMEA filter is actually getting pushed down into the join at all, or whether it's only being applied after the full join already ran -- and I'd also check whether EMEA's data specifically is hitting a worse join plan on the database side, maybe from skew or a missing index on the join columns for that segment.

But honestly, regardless of exactly what I find, my actual recommendation is almost always going to be to get off live custom SQL for this. It's opaque to Tableau's own optimization and often harder for the database's optimizer to work with than a native multi-table join configured directly in the data source. And beyond that, for something this join-heavy, I'd push to move this to an extract rather than staying live at all -- an extract does the join once, on a schedule, into Tableau's own fast engine, so every user's filtering, EMEA included, runs against an already-joined, already-fast dataset instead of re-running a live four-table join on every click. If there's a genuine hard requirement for second-by-second freshness, I'd want that confirmed explicitly rather than assumed, and only then would I fall back to native joins plus proper indexing instead of an extract.
commonMistakes: Assuming custom SQL performs identically to a native Tableau join because the SQL 'looks the same'
Not checking whether the segment filter is being applied inside the custom SQL or only in Tableau's outer wrapper
Troubleshooting purely in Tableau without pulling the actual generated SQL or database query log
Defaulting to 'add an index' without first considering whether custom SQL itself is blocking optimization
Assuming an extract isn't viable without first confirming whether true live freshness is actually required
keyPoints: Tableau wraps custom SQL in an outer query, often preventing filter pushdown into the join itself
Performance Recording or the database's query log reveals the actual generated SQL and its cost
A segment-specific timeout often points at data skew or a missing index for that segment's join pattern
Moving off custom SQL to native joins restores more optimization opportunity
An extract strategy pre-materializes the join once, removing live join cost from every user interaction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses custom SQL's filter-pushdown limitation as the likely root cause
Describes a concrete diagnostic approach using Performance Recording or query logs
Recommends a sound fix (native joins and/or extract strategy)
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: An ADF Pipeline That Fails Silently for One Source Partition Only
questions.prompt: A metadata-driven ADF pipeline ingests 50 on-prem SQL Server source tables nightly through a self-hosted integration runtime. For the past week, one specific table has simply stopped updating in the target, but the pipeline run history shows the overall pipeline succeeding every night with no failed activities. Walk through how you'd actually find what's wrong and the most likely root causes given this specific symptom pattern.
questions.modelAnswer:
A pipeline-level 'succeeded' status in a metadata-driven, ForEach-based design is specifically not proof that every individual table's copy inside that loop actually did anything meaningful -- the overall pipeline activity can report success even when one iteration of the ForEach copied zero rows, as long as that iteration didn't throw an actual error. The first move is to stop trusting the pipeline-level status and go into the specific run's activity-level output for just that table's ForEach iteration, checking the Copy Activity's own output JSON for rowsRead/rowsCopied -- if rowsCopied is consistently 0 for this table across the past week's runs while every other table shows a normal row count, that confirms the pipeline is 'succeeding' at running an empty copy, not actually succeeding at moving this table's data.

Given the metadata-driven design, the most likely root cause given exactly this symptom -- one table silently stuck, nothing else affected, no errors -- is the watermark value for that specific table's row in the control table. If last week's run for this one table failed to advance its watermark correctly (a prior transient failure that got silently swallowed, a manual edit to the control table that set the value wrong, or a type mismatch between the stored watermark and the source column making the comparison always evaluate to 'nothing new'), every subsequent run's dynamically-built WHERE clause for this table would filter using a stale or incorrect watermark and legitimately return zero new rows -- which the Copy Activity correctly reports as a successful run of zero rows, exactly matching the symptom.

The second most likely cause, specific to this being routed through a self-hosted integration runtime, is a connectivity or permission issue scoped to just this one table rather than the whole source -- for instance, if this table recently moved to a different schema or database on the source SQL Server, or its specific service account permissions were changed, while the other 49 tables' connections are unaffected; this would normally throw a real error, but if the dynamically-built source query for this table has a try/catch or a lenient error-handling pattern somewhere in the pipeline (a common anti-pattern in metadata-driven designs where a failure in one ForEach iteration is deliberately swallowed so it doesn't take down the other 49 tables' runs), that error could be getting caught and logged somewhere other than the pipeline's top-level status, explaining why the pipeline run history shows no failures.

The fix, beyond resolving whichever of these is confirmed, is to close the actual gap that let this go unnoticed for a week: add an explicit post-copy validation step in the control pipeline -- comparing rowsCopied against an expected-minimum threshold, or comparing the new watermark against the previous one to confirm it actually advanced -- and alert when a specific table's row count is zero for more than one consecutive run, since a single zero-row night can be entirely legitimate (no new data that day) but a sustained run of zeros for one specific table while 49 others behave normally is exactly the pattern that indicates a broken watermark or a swallowed error, and that distinction needs to be surfaced automatically rather than discovered a week later by someone noticing stale data downstream.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd stop trusting is the pipeline's overall success status, because in a ForEach-based metadata-driven pipeline, 'succeeded' just means no activity threw an error -- it doesn't mean every table inside that loop actually moved data. So I'd go into this specific table's ForEach iteration in the run history and look at the Copy Activity's own output for rowsCopied. If that's been sitting at zero for a week while every other table shows normal numbers, that confirms we're 'succeeding' at copying nothing for this one table, not actually succeeding.

Given it's just this one table and nothing else, my first suspect is the watermark value in the control table for that specific row. If it got stuck at a stale value -- from a silently-swallowed failure last week, a bad manual edit, or a type mismatch that makes the comparison always come back empty -- every run since then would correctly build a WHERE clause that legitimately finds nothing new, and the Copy Activity reports that as a clean, successful, zero-row run. That matches the symptom exactly.

My second suspect, since this is going through a self-hosted integration runtime, is something scoped to just this table on the source side -- maybe it moved schemas, or a permission changed for just this table's access path. Normally that would throw a real error, but if there's error-handling somewhere in the pipeline that's deliberately swallowing per-table failures so one bad table doesn't take down the other 49, that error could be getting caught and logged somewhere that never bubbles up to the pipeline's top-level status.

Either way, the real fix isn't just resolving this one table -- it's closing the gap that let it go unnoticed for a week. I'd add an explicit check after each table's copy that flags when rowsCopied is zero for more than one consecutive run, or when the watermark didn't actually advance, and alert on that specifically. A single zero-row night can be totally legitimate; a sustained run of zeros for one table while forty-nine others look normal is exactly the pattern that should trigger an alert automatically instead of being found a week later by someone noticing stale numbers downstream.
commonMistakes: Trusting pipeline-level success status as proof every ForEach iteration moved data
Not checking the Copy Activity's own rowsCopied output for the specific affected table
Assuming a stuck watermark would necessarily throw an error rather than silently return zero rows
Not considering that error-swallowing logic built to isolate one table's failure can also hide the evidence of that failure
Fixing this one table's issue without adding monitoring to catch the same pattern automatically in the future
keyPoints: Pipeline-level success does not guarantee every ForEach iteration moved meaningful data
Copy Activity output (rowsCopied) for the specific table's run is the key diagnostic signal
A stuck or incorrect watermark is the most likely cause of a silent, error-free zero-row pattern
Error-handling designed to isolate per-table failures can also suppress visibility into them
A sustained zero-row streak for one table, while others are normal, should trigger an automated alert

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that pipeline-level success masks per-table zero-row copies
Describes a concrete diagnostic approach using activity-level output
Correctly identifies a stuck watermark as the most likely root cause
Proposes monitoring/alerting to close the detection gap going forward

questions.title: Snowflake Compute Costs Tripled With No Change in Data Volume
questions.prompt: A Snowflake account's monthly compute bill has tripled over two months with no meaningful growth in data volume or user count. Walk through how you'd use Query Profile and account usage views to actually find the cause, and the three most common root causes you'd specifically check for.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first move is quantitative, not anecdotal: query SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY (or the equivalent in ORGANIZATION_USAGE for multi-account views) grouped by warehouse and day over the period the cost tripled, to see whether the increase is concentrated in one specific warehouse or spread evenly -- a concentrated spike points at a specific workload or job change, while an even spread across all warehouses more often points at a sizing or scaling policy change applied broadly. Once a specific warehouse is implicated, QUERY_HISTORY filtered to that warehouse and time range, sorted by total_elapsed_time or credits_used_cloud_services, surfaces the specific queries actually driving the cost.

The three most common root causes, in roughly the order I'd check them: first, a warehouse size or auto-scaling (multi-cluster) configuration change -- someone resized a warehouse up, or changed MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT/MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT on a multi-cluster warehouse, intentionally or by someone copying a config from a different environment, and now routine workloads are running on larger or more concurrent compute than before with no corresponding change in actual work being done; this shows up clearly in WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY as a step change in credits-per-hour coinciding with a specific date. Second, a specific query or job regressed -- a scheduled task, a dbt model, or a BI tool's refresh query that used to run efficiently started doing something expensive, most often due to a clustering/pruning failure (the exact scenario where micro-partition pruning stopped working because of how data is landing, covered separately) or a join that used to be selective becoming a full scan because of a data skew change or a missing statistics-driven plan change; Query Profile on the specific slow query shows this directly via the percentage of partitions scanned versus pruned, and a sudden jump in bytes scanned for a query that logically shouldn't be scanning more is the smoking gun. Third, auto-suspend either being disabled or set to an impractically long timeout on a warehouse that used to suspend quickly between uses -- a warehouse sitting idle-but-billing for long stretches between small queries looks identical to a legitimate workload increase in a simple total-credits view, and only becomes obvious when you look at the ratio of actual query execution time to total warehouse uptime for that period.

Once the specific cause is confirmed through one of those three lenses, the fix is targeted rather than a blanket 'turn everything down,' which risks breaking something that genuinely needed the extra compute: right-size the warehouse back down and validate query performance doesn't regress unacceptably, fix the specific query/job that regressed (often a clustering key or query rewrite, not a warehouse size change at all), or tighten auto-suspend back to a sensible value (60 seconds is a common default to return to from an inflated setting) while confirming that doesn't reintroduce excessive cold-start overhead for legitimately frequent, bursty workloads.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't start guessing -- I'd start with WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY, grouped by warehouse and day across the period the bill tripled, to see if the increase is concentrated in one warehouse or spread across everything. Concentrated points at something specific that changed -- a job, a config. Spread-out more often points at something applied broadly, like a sizing policy change rolled out everywhere.

Once I've got a specific warehouse, I'd pull QUERY_HISTORY for that warehouse and time window sorted by elapsed time or credits, to find the actual queries driving the spend. From there, three things I'd specifically check, in this order: first, did someone resize the warehouse or change its multi-cluster min/max settings -- that shows up as a clean step change in credits-per-hour on a specific date, and it's a surprisingly common cause, often someone copying a config from another environment without meaning to change production spend. Second, did a specific recurring query or job regress -- a dbt model, a scheduled task, a BI refresh -- usually because pruning stopped working on a table it used to scan efficiently, or a join that used to be selective turned into something closer to a full scan. Query Profile shows this directly as a jump in partitions scanned versus pruned for that specific query. Third, and this one's sneaky because it looks identical to 'more usage' in a simple credits chart, is auto-suspend being disabled or set way too long -- a warehouse sitting idle but still billing between small queries racks up cost that has nothing to do with actual work being done.

Whichever of those three it turns out to be, I'd fix that specific thing rather than just turning everything down across the board, because an across-the-board cut risks breaking something that genuinely needed the extra compute for a legitimate reason.
commonMistakes: Jumping to 'just resize everything down' without first identifying which warehouse or query is actually responsible
Not distinguishing a concentrated cost spike (specific cause) from an evenly spread increase (broad policy change)
Overlooking auto-suspend misconfiguration because idle-but-billing time looks identical to real usage in a simple credits chart
Not using Query Profile's partition scanned/pruned metrics to confirm a pruning regression as the root cause
Treating a warehouse resize as purely a cost lever without validating the performance impact of resizing back down
keyPoints: WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY grouped by warehouse/day localizes whether the cost increase is concentrated or spread
QUERY_HISTORY surfaces the specific queries actually driving cost once a warehouse is implicated
Warehouse size/multi-cluster configuration changes are a common and easily detected root cause
Query/job regressions (often pruning failures) show up directly in Query Profile's scanned-vs-pruned metrics
Auto-suspend misconfiguration causes idle-but-billing time that looks like usage growth in simple cost views

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a correct, concrete diagnostic approach using metering/query history views
Correctly identifies and explains warehouse sizing/scaling config changes as a root cause
Correctly identifies and explains a query/pruning regression as a root cause
Correctly identifies and explains auto-suspend misconfiguration as a root cause

questions.title: dbt Slim CI Runs Everything Even Though Only One Model Changed
questions.prompt: A dbt project's Slim CI job is supposed to only build and test models affected by a pull request's changes, using state:modified+. Instead, every PR triggers a full rebuild of all 400 models, defeating the purpose of Slim CI and burning warehouse credits on every commit. Walk through the likely causes and how you'd confirm which one is actually happening.
questions.modelAnswer:
state:modified+ only works at all if dbt actually has a valid prior manifest.json to diff the current project against -- the entire mechanism is a comparison between the current run's compiled state and a previously-stored state artifact representing the last successful production (or otherwise designated) run. The single most common cause of this symptom is that the CI job isn't actually retrieving a real prior manifest at all: either the --state flag is pointing at a stale, empty, or missing directory (a misconfigured artifact download step, a path that doesn't exist on this particular CI runner, or a deploy job that never actually succeeded in publishing its manifest to the expected location), or the CI job is comparing against a manifest from an unrelated or very old run rather than the most recent successful deploy -- in either case, if dbt can't find a meaningful comparison manifest, state:modified+ selection effectively has nothing valid to diff against and either errors (which should have been noticed) or, depending on exact dbt Cloud/dbt Core CLI configuration, silently falls back to behaving as if everything is new/modified.

The second common cause is dbt_project.yml-level or environment-level non-determinism that makes every single model's compiled SQL look different from the stored manifest even when the model's own source file didn't change -- a Jinja macro referencing run_started_at or another non-deterministic value inside a model that gets compiled into many or all models via a shared macro, an environment variable that differs between the CI environment and the environment the baseline manifest was generated in (different target schema names baked into compiled SQL, different var() values), or a dbt version mismatch between the CI job and whatever generated the stored manifest, which can change how models compile even with identical source. Any of these makes dbt's state comparison correctly detect every model as 'different' from the stored manifest, because the compiled artifact genuinely is different -- it's not a bug in state comparison, it's that the inputs to compilation aren't actually stable between the baseline and the CI run.

To confirm which one is actually happening: first verify the manifest artifact being passed to --state genuinely exists, is recent, and corresponds to the actual last successful production run -- not a guess, actually open it and check its generated_at timestamp and dbt version against what the CI job is running. If that checks out, run dbt run --select state:modified+ --state path/to/manifest locally against that same manifest and compare the selection output to what CI produces; if local selection correctly picks only the changed model but CI selects everything, the problem is CI-environment-specific (environment variables, dbt version, or the artifact retrieval step itself), not the state logic. If local selection also picks everything despite only one file actually changing, use dbt compile with --select state:modified+ and manually diff the compiled SQL for an unrelated model between the current compile and the baseline manifest -- if that compiled SQL differs for a model whose source didn't change, that's direct evidence of the environment/non-determinism cause rather than a manifest-retrieval problem.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The whole mechanism behind state:modified+ depends on dbt actually having a real, recent manifest from the last successful run to diff against -- so my first question is always whether that manifest is genuinely being retrieved correctly in CI. A huge number of 'Slim CI isn't working' cases I've seen come down to the --state path pointing at something stale, empty, or just the wrong run -- a broken artifact download step, a deploy job that silently didn't actually succeed in publishing its manifest where CI expects to find it. If there's no valid baseline to compare against, dbt either has nothing meaningful to diff or ends up treating everything as changed.

The other common cause, if the manifest retrieval genuinely checks out, is that something about the compiled SQL itself isn't stable between the baseline and the CI run -- a macro using something non-deterministic like run_started_at that gets compiled into a lot of models, an environment variable or var() that differs between CI and wherever the baseline was generated, or even a dbt version mismatch changing how things compile. In that case state comparison isn't broken, it's correctly reporting that the compiled output genuinely differs -- the problem is upstream of state comparison, in what's feeding it.

To actually confirm which one it is, I'd start by literally opening the manifest CI is using and checking its timestamp and dbt version against what's expected. Then I'd run the same state:modified+ selection locally against that same manifest -- if locally it correctly picks just the one changed model but CI picks everything, that's a CI-environment problem, not a dbt logic problem. If it fails locally too, I'd compile with state:modified+ and diff the compiled SQL for some unrelated, unchanged model against the baseline manifest -- if that SQL is actually different, that's hard evidence it's a non-determinism or environment-variable issue, not a missing-manifest issue.
commonMistakes: Assuming state:modified+ is broken rather than checking whether a valid baseline manifest is actually being retrieved
Not verifying the manifest's generated_at timestamp and dbt version against the CI run's expectations
Overlooking non-deterministic Jinja (like run_started_at) compiled into many models as a cause of false-positive 'modified' detection
Not reproducing the selection locally against the same manifest to isolate whether the problem is CI-environment-specific
Assuming a dbt version mismatch between CI and the baseline-generating job couldn't affect compiled SQL output
keyPoints: state:modified+ requires a valid, recent baseline manifest to diff against
A missing, stale, or mis-pathed manifest is the most common root cause of Slim CI rebuilding everything
Non-deterministic macros or differing environment variables/dbt versions can make compiled SQL genuinely differ, correctly triggering full selection
Confirming the manifest's validity and reproducing selection locally isolates whether the cause is CI-environment-specific or compilation non-determinism
State comparison working 'correctly' on an invalid or unstable baseline still produces an unusable result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing/stale/mis-pathed manifest as the most likely root cause
Correctly identifies non-deterministic compilation/environment drift as a secondary cause
Describes a concrete, logical diagnostic sequence to confirm which cause applies
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Fabric Capacity Throttling a Critical Executive Dashboard During Month-End
questions.prompt: On the last business day of every month, an executive-facing Power BI dashboard on a shared Fabric F64 capacity becomes unusably slow or outright fails to refresh, while the same dashboard performs fine every other day. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a capacity contention issue rather than a model or query problem, and the concrete steps you'd take, both immediately and structurally, to prevent it next month-end.
questions.modelAnswer:
The pattern itself -- fine every day except one predictable, calendar-driven day -- is already strong evidence against a model or query problem, since neither the dashboard's DAX nor its underlying data model changes based on the day of the month; if the same report, same queries, same data volume behaves differently only on month-end, the variable is almost certainly something else happening on the shared capacity at the same time, not the dashboard itself. The confirmation step is the Fabric Capacity Metrics app, specifically looking at the interactive and background utilization timelines for that F64 capacity on the last several month-ends versus a normal day, and cross-referencing any throttling or rejected-operation events logged against this specific semantic model's refresh or query activity during that window -- if utilization spikes and throttling events cluster specifically around month-end and specifically overlap with when other workloads (month-end financial close jobs, large batch Spark pipelines, a flood of ad hoc report refreshes from finance) are also running on the same shared capacity, that's the direct confirmation this is capacity contention, not the dashboard's own design.

The immediate fix for the next occurrence, if there's lead time before the next month-end, is workload isolation: moving this specific executive dashboard's semantic model to its own dedicated capacity (or at minimum into a workspace assigned to a capacity with guaranteed headroom away from the colliding month-end batch jobs), so its refresh and query activity are no longer competing for the same CU pool as the heavy month-end workloads. If a dedicated capacity isn't immediately available, a tactical fix is rescheduling the competing batch jobs (the Spark pipelines, other heavy refreshes) to run at a different time than the executive dashboard's own refresh window specifically on month-end, even if that's not ideal the rest of the month, to stop the two workloads from colliding on the one day they currently do.

The structural fix, beyond this specific incident, is actual capacity planning rather than reactive firefighting: using the Fabric Capacity Metrics app's historical data to model peak -- not average -- utilization across the full month, specifically identifying recurring high-load windows like month-end close, and sizing (or architecting workload placement across multiple capacities) based on that peak rather than the comfortable-looking daily average, which is exactly the trap that let this go unnoticed until it became a visible executive-facing incident. This should also include setting up proactive alerting on capacity utilization and throttling events so the next month-end contention issue, on this dashboard or any other, is caught by monitoring before an executive notices a slow dashboard, rather than after.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The pattern alone -- same dashboard, same data, breaks only on one predictable calendar day every month -- already tells me this probably isn't the dashboard's own fault, because nothing about its DAX or its model changes based on the date. Something else happening on the same shared capacity at month-end is almost certainly the real variable.

To confirm it, I'd go to the Fabric Capacity Metrics app and look at utilization and any throttling events for this F64 capacity specifically around the last few month-ends versus a normal day, and check whether those spikes line up with this dashboard's own refresh and query activity. If I see utilization spiking and throttling events clustering right when month-end close jobs or other heavy batch work are also running on the same capacity, that confirms it's contention, not a model problem.

For the immediate fix, if I've got any lead time before next month-end, I'd push to move this specific executive-facing semantic model onto its own dedicated capacity, or at least into a workspace that's got guaranteed headroom away from whatever's colliding with it. If that's not realistic on short notice, the tactical move is just rescheduling the competing batch jobs so they're not running at the same time as this dashboard's refresh window on that one day, even if that's not how we'd want to run things the rest of the month.

Beyond patching this one incident, I'd want to actually do real capacity planning off this -- use the Capacity Metrics app's history to look at peak load across the month, not the average, specifically flagging recurring spikes like month-end close, and size or split capacity based on that peak. I'd also set up proactive alerting on utilization and throttling so the next time this kind of contention starts building, it gets caught by monitoring before an executive notices a slow dashboard, not after.
commonMistakes: Treating a calendar-predictable slowdown as a model/query problem and tuning DAX that was never the issue
Not using the Fabric Capacity Metrics app to confirm contention before proposing a fix
Sizing capacity based on average utilization rather than peak/recurring high-load windows
Fixing the immediate incident without setting up proactive alerting to catch the next occurrence earlier
Assuming workload isolation (dedicated capacity) is always the only viable fix, without considering job rescheduling as a lower-cost interim option
keyPoints: A calendar-predictable slowdown with unchanged model/queries points at capacity contention, not the dashboard itself
The Fabric Capacity Metrics app confirms contention via utilization spikes and throttling events at the relevant time
Workload isolation (dedicated capacity or workspace placement) is the structural fix for competing high-priority workloads
Job rescheduling is a viable tactical fix when immediate capacity isolation isn't available
Proper capacity planning requires modeling peak, not average, utilization across recurring high-load periods

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that a calendar-predictable pattern points at capacity contention
Describes a concrete confirmation approach using the Capacity Metrics app
Proposes a sound immediate fix (isolation or rescheduling)
Proposes a sound structural fix (peak-based capacity planning and alerting)

questions.title: A Delta Table That Keeps Getting Slower Despite Nightly OPTIMIZE
questions.prompt: A Delta table ingested by a streaming MERGE job runs a nightly OPTIMIZE job, yet query performance has steadily degraded over three months. You check and confirm OPTIMIZE is actually completing successfully every night with no errors. Walk through what else could be going wrong and how you'd confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A completing OPTIMIZE job doesn't guarantee the table's actual query performance problem is being addressed, because OPTIMIZE without Z-ORDER only does file compaction (bin-packing small files into fewer, larger ones) -- it says nothing about whether data relevant to the queries actually filtering this table is physically co-located within those larger files. If the queries hitting this table filter on, say, CustomerRegion or EventType and OPTIMIZE has never been given a ZORDER BY clause naming those columns, compaction alone doesn't improve data skipping for those filters at all -- you'd have fewer, bigger files, each one still containing a wide, unclustered mix of every region and event type, so file-level min/max pruning for those filters stays just as ineffective as before, and any apparent 'OPTIMIZE should be helping' assumption is based on compaction, which is a different problem than skipping effectiveness.

The second thing to check is whether VACUUM is running at all, separately from OPTIMIZE -- a successful OPTIMIZE marks old small files as logically removed in the _delta_log but does not physically delete them; without a corresponding VACUUM, every night's compaction adds another batch of now-orphaned files sitting in cloud storage, and over three months of nightly MERGE-plus-OPTIMIZE with no VACUUM, the sheer number of objects stored under that table's path can grow large enough that cloud-storage-level operations (listing files during planning, or query engines that have to reconcile a larger set of referenced-vs-actually-present files) slow down independent of the logical table's actual data size -- this shows up as a growing discrepancy between the table's logical row count/size and the actual object count or storage footprint under its path.

The third thing, specific to a streaming MERGE workload, is checking whether the table's transaction log itself has grown large enough to slow down planning -- a MERGE running frequently (say every few minutes) generates a new log entry per run, and while Delta checkpoints periodically to avoid replaying the full history, if checkpoint generation has silently stopped working (a permissions issue, a version incompatibility) or the checkpoint interval is miscalibrated for this run frequency, every query might be paying an increasingly expensive log-replay cost on top of whatever file-layout issue also exists, which compounds with the other two causes rather than being mutually exclusive with them.

Confirming all three is a matter of checking: DESCRIBE HISTORY or the OPTIMIZE command's own logged parameters to see whether ZORDER BY was ever actually specified and on which columns, versus what the actual query patterns filter on (via query history/logs); whether VACUUM has run at all recently and comparing the table's logical size against its actual file/object count on storage; and checking for the presence and recency of _delta_log checkpoint files relative to the commit frequency. Given a three-month gradual degradation with OPTIMIZE technically succeeding throughout, the most likely single answer is the first one -- OPTIMIZE running without Z-ORDER on the columns queries actually filter by, which means the file-count problem has been 'fixed' every night while the data-skipping problem it was actually supposed to help with never was.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that OPTIMIZE is completing successfully doesn't actually tell me the real problem is being solved, because plain OPTIMIZE without a ZORDER clause only does file compaction -- it bin-packs small files into bigger ones, but it says nothing about whether the data inside those bigger files is actually clustered by whatever columns the queries are filtering on. If nobody ever specified ZORDER BY on the columns these queries actually use, every file still has a wide mix of everything in it, and data skipping stays just as ineffective as before compaction -- we fixed the small-files problem and never touched the pruning problem, which might be the actual bottleneck.

Second thing I'd check, completely separately, is whether VACUUM has been running at all. OPTIMIZE marks old small files as logically gone but doesn't physically delete them -- only VACUUM does that. Three months of nightly compaction with no VACUUM means three months of orphaned files piling up in storage, and at some point that sheer object count starts slowing down things like file listing during query planning, independent of how much actual data is in the table logically.

Third, since this is a frequent streaming MERGE, I'd check the transaction log itself -- if checkpoint generation has quietly broken or isn't keeping pace with how often MERGE is committing, queries could be paying an increasingly expensive log-replay cost just to figure out current table state, on top of whatever file-layout issue is also going on.

I'd check all three, but given it's a slow three-month creep with OPTIMIZE technically succeeding the whole time, my first bet is the ZORDER gap -- we've been running maintenance that fixes a problem that isn't the real bottleneck, while the actual pruning problem query performance depends on was never addressed.
commonMistakes: Assuming OPTIMIZE automatically improves data skipping even without a ZORDER clause on relevant columns
Not checking whether VACUUM is running at all, separately from OPTIMIZE's success
Overlooking transaction log/checkpoint health as a contributor to query planning slowdown on a high-frequency MERGE table
Treating 'the maintenance job succeeded' as equivalent to 'the maintenance addressed the actual performance problem'
Fixing one of the three causes and declaring victory without checking whether the others are also contributing
keyPoints: OPTIMIZE without ZORDER compacts files but does not improve data skipping for query filters
VACUUM must run separately to reclaim storage from files OPTIMIZE has logically superseded
A frequent-MERGE table's transaction log and checkpoint health can independently degrade query planning
All three causes should be checked, since they compound rather than being mutually exclusive
A successfully-completing maintenance job is not proof that the actual performance bottleneck is being addressed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing ZORDER as the likely primary cause
Correctly identifies missing VACUUM as a contributing cause
Correctly identifies transaction log/checkpoint health as a possible contributing cause
Describes a concrete way to confirm each hypothesis

questions.title: A Streaming Pipeline Producing Duplicate Rows in the Gold Table
questions.prompt: A Structured Streaming job reads from Kafka, applies a transformation, and writes upserts into a gold Delta table. After a cluster restart last week caused by a spot-instance eviction, finance noticed duplicate revenue being counted for a handful of transactions around the restart window. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix, distinguishing between what Spark's checkpointing is supposed to guarantee and where the actual gap is.
questions.modelAnswer:
Spark Structured Streaming's checkpointing mechanism is designed to give exactly-once processing guarantees for the combination of 'reading from the source' and 'writing to the sink,' but that guarantee depends on both the source and the sink actually participating correctly in the checkpoint-and-recovery protocol -- and a MERGE-based upsert into Delta is specifically designed to support this correctly as long as the write itself is idempotent with respect to a stable key, which is exactly where this scenario's gap most likely lives. When the cluster was evicted mid-batch, Spark's recovery process restarts from the last committed checkpoint offset, which should mean: any micro-batch that had fully committed before the eviction is not reprocessed, and any micro-batch that was in progress but not yet committed gets reprocessed from its starting offset. If the MERGE's upsert key genuinely and uniquely identifies each transaction, reprocessing that in-flight batch should just re-apply the same upserts idempotently with no duplication -- the second run of the same batch should match and update the same existing rows, not insert new ones.

The actual gap, given duplicates specifically appeared around the restart window, is most likely one of two things. First, and most common: the MERGE's matching key isn't actually a stable, unique identifier for each transaction -- if it's keyed on something derived at transformation time rather than a genuinely stable upstream transaction ID (for instance, a key that includes a processing timestamp, or a composite key that isn't actually guaranteed unique per transaction), then reprocessing the same underlying Kafka messages after the restart produces rows that don't match the already-written rows from the partially-committed batch, so MERGE's NOT MATCHED branch inserts them as new rows instead of correctly recognizing and updating the existing ones -- that's a correctness bug in the merge key, not a checkpointing failure. Second: if the write path isn't actually a single atomic MERGE but something closer to a foreachBatch implementation with multiple separate write steps, or a sink that doesn't support transactional commit semantics tied to the checkpoint offset, the checkpoint can advance past a batch whose write only partially completed, which would also produce exactly this kind of narrow, restart-window-specific duplication.

Confirming which one it is: pull the actual duplicate transaction records and check whether their natural/business key (not just the MERGE's technical matching key) is identical across the duplicate rows -- if it is, and the MERGE's ON clause doesn't use that same key, that's the smoking gun for a merge-key bug. Checking the Spark driver logs and the streaming query's checkpoint directory for the specific offsets committed immediately before and after the eviction also confirms whether the same source offset range was processed twice (expected and fine, if the sink is idempotent) or whether there's evidence of a partial write that the checkpoint incorrectly treated as committed. The fix, once confirmed as a merge-key issue, is to rebuild the MERGE's ON clause around the actual stable, unique upstream transaction identifier (deduplicating within a single micro-batch first via a window function if the same key can legitimately appear more than once within one batch), which makes the entire pipeline correctly idempotent across any future restart, not just resilient to clean shutdowns.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by being precise about what checkpointing is actually supposed to guarantee here, because it's easy to blame checkpointing itself when the real problem is usually somewhere else. Structured Streaming's checkpoint-and-recovery is designed to give exactly-once semantics for source-to-sink processing, but that promise only holds if the sink write is actually idempotent with respect to a stable key -- and a MERGE into Delta is built to support exactly that, as long as the merge key genuinely, uniquely identifies each transaction.

So after the eviction, Spark should restart from the last committed offset -- anything fully committed before the crash shouldn't reprocess, and anything in flight should reprocess from where it started. If the merge key is solid, reprocessing that in-flight batch should just re-upsert the same rows and update them, not duplicate them. Given duplicates showed up specifically around the restart window, my first suspect is that the merge key isn't actually a stable, unique transaction identifier -- maybe it's got something derived at transformation time baked into it, or it's a composite key that isn't truly unique per transaction. If that's the case, reprocessing the same underlying messages produces rows that don't match what was already written from the partially-committed batch, and MERGE's not-matched branch just inserts them as new rows instead of recognizing them as the same transaction. That's a correctness bug in how the merge is keyed, not a checkpointing failure.

The other thing I'd rule out is whether the actual write path is a clean atomic MERGE at all, or something closer to multiple separate steps inside a foreachBatch that could let the checkpoint advance past a write that only partially completed.

To confirm, I'd pull the actual duplicate rows and check if their real business key -- not the technical merge key -- is identical across them. If it is, and the MERGE's ON clause isn't using that same key, that's the answer. I'd also check the checkpoint directory and driver logs around the eviction to see exactly which offsets got reprocessed. Once confirmed, the fix is rebuilding the MERGE around the actual stable transaction ID, and deduplicating within a single micro-batch first if that same ID can legitimately show up more than once in one batch -- that makes the whole pipeline genuinely idempotent against any future restart, not just lucky so far.
commonMistakes: Blaming Spark checkpointing itself rather than checking whether the sink write is actually idempotent
Assuming any MERGE statement automatically guarantees idempotency regardless of what the ON clause actually keys on
Not distinguishing the technical merge key from the true business/transaction key when diagnosing duplicates
Overlooking foreachBatch implementations with multiple non-atomic write steps as a separate source of the same symptom
Fixing the immediate duplicates without rebuilding the merge key to prevent recurrence on the next restart
keyPoints: Checkpointing guarantees exactly-once processing only when the sink write is genuinely idempotent on a stable key
A merge key that isn't a true, stable, unique transaction identifier causes reprocessed batches to insert duplicates instead of upserting
Non-atomic foreachBatch write paths can also let the checkpoint advance past a partially-completed write
Comparing the true business key across duplicate rows against the MERGE's actual ON clause isolates the root cause
The durable fix is rebuilding the merge key around a stable transaction identifier, with intra-batch deduplication if needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Structured Streaming checkpointing does and does not guarantee by itself
Correctly diagnoses an unstable/incorrect merge key as the likely root cause
Describes a concrete diagnostic approach to confirm the cause
Proposes a durable fix that prevents recurrence on future restarts

questions.title: A Deadlock Victim Pattern That Only Appears During Nightly Batch Load
questions.prompt: Every night around 2 AM, a handful of ad hoc reporting sessions get killed with deadlock victim errors (error 1205), always at roughly the same time the ETL batch load window runs. Walk through how you'd pull and read the actual deadlock graph, what pattern you'd expect to see given this timing, and the specific production fix you'd propose versus one you'd avoid.
questions.modelAnswer:
The timing correlation -- deadlocks clustering specifically during the batch load window, not randomly throughout the day -- is the first real clue, and it points strongly at a lock-ordering conflict between the batch load's write pattern and the reporting sessions' read pattern rather than a logic bug in either one individually. The deadlock graph itself (pulled from the system_health Extended Events session, which captures deadlocks automatically with zero extra setup, via SSMS's built-in XEvent viewer or a query against the ring buffer target) shows two process nodes, each one's held locks and requested locks, and the resources (object, index, specific key/page) involved; what I'd expect to see given this timing is the batch load process holding an exclusive or update lock on a resource the reporting query needs a shared lock on, while the reporting query simultaneously holds a shared lock on a different resource the batch load needs to extend its own lock onto next -- a classic cyclic wait where each side is progressing through the same table or index in a different order, which large batch operations (inserting/updating many rows across a wide key range) are especially prone to triggering against concurrent readers scanning the same range.

The deadlock monitor picks a victim based on a combination of factors (transaction log bytes written, to minimize rollback cost, with session priority as a tiebreaker), and ad hoc reporting sessions getting killed specifically, every night, strongly suggests they're consistently landing on the lower-cost-to-roll-back side of that calculation relative to the batch load -- which also means the batch load transaction is probably not failing and retrying, it's the reporting side bearing all the visible pain while the actual root cause (both sides fighting over the same rows under locking concurrency) goes unaddressed because nobody notices a transaction that quietly wins every time.

The fix I'd propose is READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT at the database level, which removes the reporting sessions' shared locks from the picture entirely by letting them read from a versioned snapshot instead of taking blocking locks -- this breaks the deadlock cycle without touching the ETL batch load's own locking behavior at all, since the batch load's writes were never really the problem in isolation, it's the collision with concurrent readers that is. The fix I'd specifically avoid is reflexively adding NOLOCK hints to the reporting queries as a quick patch: that does stop the deadlocks, but it does so by letting those reports read uncommitted, potentially inconsistent data mid-batch-load -- for a nightly ETL window that's actively inserting and updating rows, that risks reports silently showing partially-loaded or logically inconsistent numbers, which trades a loud, visible error (the deadlock) for a quiet, much worse one (a wrong number nobody notices), and shouldn't be the production fix even though it would technically make the error messages stop.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that this happens specifically during the batch window every night, not randomly, is the big clue -- that's not a logic bug in either process individually, it's the two of them colliding on lock ordering when they run concurrently.

I'd pull the actual deadlock graph out of system_health, since it captures these automatically, and look at the two process nodes -- what each one's holding, what each one's waiting for, and on which specific resources. Given the timing, I'd expect to see the batch load holding a lock the reporting query needs while the reporting query holds something the batch load needs next -- a classic cyclic wait, which big batch writes are especially prone to triggering against concurrent reads scanning the same range in a different order.

The deadlock monitor picks whichever side is cheaper to roll back as the victim, and if it's consistently the ad hoc reporting sessions dying every single night, that tells me the batch load transaction is basically always winning that calculation -- which also means nobody's noticing the actual root cause, because the batch side never visibly fails, only the reporting side does.

My actual fix would be READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT at the database level -- it takes the reporting sessions' shared locks out of the equation entirely by having them read from a versioned snapshot instead, which breaks the cycle without touching the ETL logic at all, since the batch writes weren't really the problem on their own. What I'd specifically push back on is just slapping NOLOCK on the reporting queries to make the errors go away -- that does stop the deadlocks, but it does it by letting those reports read uncommitted data in the middle of an active load, which trades a loud error everyone notices for a quiet wrong number that nobody does. That's a worse outcome dressed up as a fix.

Not pulling the actual deadlock graph before proposing a fix
Defaulting to NOLOCK as the production fix without weighing the data-consistency risk during an active load window
Assuming the batch load transaction must also be failing just because the reporting side is visibly erroring
Not recognizing the deadlock victim-selection criteria (log bytes written) as the reason one side consistently loses
keyPoints: Deadlocks clustering at a specific recurring time point at lock-ordering conflict between two concurrent workloads
The deadlock graph from system_health shows the exact held/requested locks and resources for both sides
The deadlock victim is chosen by lowest rollback cost, which can make one side consistently lose every time
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT removes the reporting side's blocking locks, breaking the cycle without changing ETL logic
