questions.title: Row-Level Security Letting a User See Rows They Shouldn't
questions.prompt: A Power BI report with RLS configured through a USERPRINCIPALNAME()-based role shows one specific regional manager data from a region they should not have access to, but only when they drill into a specific visual, not on the report's landing page. Walk through how you'd diagnose this, including the specific DAX/relationship issue most likely responsible.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fact that the leak is specific to one visual rather than universal across the whole report is the key clue: if the RLS role's filter expression itself were simply wrong (a bad USERPRINCIPALNAME() mapping, or a typo in the region comparison logic), the leak would be universal across every visual on every page, because RLS applies its filter at the table level, consistently, regardless of which visual is querying it. A leak isolated to one specific visual on drill-through strongly suggests the RLS filter is being correctly applied to its target table, but that filter isn't actually propagating through to whatever table the misbehaving visual is really querying -- which is almost always a relationship direction or an ALLEXCEPT/ALL-type filter-removal issue inside a measure used specifically on that visual, not a problem with the RLS rule itself.

The first thing I'd check is exactly which table the RLS role's filter expression is defined on, and then check whether that table has a single-direction relationship that doesn't reach the table(s) the specific misbehaving visual is pulling from. If RLS filters the Region dimension table but a measure on this one visual uses CALCULATE with ALL() or REMOVEFILTERS() over a table that sits on the "many" side of a relationship without bidirectional filtering back to Region, that measure can inadvertently strip out the RLS-propagated filter for its own calculation -- RLS filters are implemented as regular filter context, and any DAX that explicitly clears filters (ALL, REMOVEFILTERS, ALLEXCEPT without preserving the right columns) on a table RLS depends on will clear the RLS filter along with everything else it was targeting, unless the measure's author was specifically careful to preserve it.

Testing this concretely means using Power BI Desktop's 'View As' role feature (or testing with the actual security role applied) specifically on the misbehaving visual in isolation, then checking each measure used by that visual for ALL/ALLEXCEPT/REMOVEFILTERS patterns that might be touching the RLS-filtered table or a table related to it. Once found, the fix is almost never to touch the RLS rule itself (which is correctly defined, that's why the landing page behaves) -- it's to rewrite the offending measure to use a narrower filter-removal pattern (ALLEXCEPT naming the specific columns that need clearing while explicitly preserving the ones RLS depends on, or KEEPFILTERS combined with the override) so that measure's business logic still works as intended without collaterally undoing the security filter it was never supposed to touch in the first place. This is exactly why any measure using ALL-family functions anywhere in a model with RLS needs a specific security-review pass -- the two features interact in a way that's easy to break accidentally and dangerous to leave unnoticed.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that really points me somewhere specific is that this only happens on one visual, not the whole report. If the RLS rule itself were wrong, I'd expect the leak everywhere, on every page, because RLS applies at the table level consistently no matter what's querying it. A leak that's isolated to one visual tells me the RLS filter is probably being applied correctly to its target table, but something specific to that one visual's measure is stripping it back out before the final result gets computed.

So I'd go look at exactly which measure that visual uses, and specifically whether it's using ALL, ALLEXCEPT, or REMOVEFILTERS anywhere that touches the table RLS is defined on, or a table related to it. RLS filters are just regular filter context under the hood -- so if a measure explicitly clears filters on that table for its own business logic and isn't careful to preserve the RLS-driven filter while doing it, it can accidentally wipe out the security filter along with whatever it actually meant to clear.

To confirm it, I'd use View As Role on just that visual in isolation and trace through each measure it depends on looking for exactly that pattern. Once I find it, I almost never touch the RLS rule itself -- it's working fine everywhere else, that's the tell. I'd fix the measure instead, usually by narrowing the ALLEXCEPT to name only the columns that actually need clearing while explicitly keeping the ones RLS depends on. And honestly, this is the kind of thing that makes me want a standing rule: any model that has RLS turned on needs every measure using an ALL-family function specifically reviewed for this interaction, because it's a very easy thing to break by accident and a genuinely dangerous one to leave unnoticed.
commonMistakes: Assuming a visual-specific RLS leak means the RLS rule itself is wrong, when a universal leak would be the symptom of that
Not checking ALL/ALLEXCEPT/REMOVEFILTERS usage in the specific misbehaving visual's measures
Fixing the RLS rule when the actual bug is a measure stripping the RLS filter via an overly broad filter-removal function
Not using View As Role to isolate and test the specific visual in question
Failing to establish an ongoing review process for ALL-family DAX functions in models that rely on RLS
keyPoints: A leak isolated to one visual, not the whole report, points at a measure issue, not the RLS rule itself
RLS filters are implemented as ordinary filter context and can be stripped by ALL/ALLEXCEPT/REMOVEFILTERS
View As Role on the specific visual isolates and confirms the issue
The fix is narrowing the offending measure's filter-removal logic, not touching the RLS rule
Models with RLS need an ongoing review process for any measure using ALL-family functions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that a visual-isolated leak points at a measure, not the RLS rule
Correctly identifies ALL/ALLEXCEPT/REMOVEFILTERS stripping RLS filter context as the mechanism
Describes a concrete diagnostic approach using View As Role
Proposes the correct, narrowly-scoped fix

questions.title: dbt Tests Failing Intermittently and Nobody Trusts the CI Pipeline Anymore
questions.prompt: A dbt project's not_null and relationships tests on a core fact table fail intermittently, roughly one run in five, with no apparent pattern, and the team has started just re-running CI until it passes. Walk through how you'd distinguish a genuinely flaky test from a real, intermittent data quality issue, and what you'd do about the team's current 're-run until green' habit.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing to establish is that 'intermittent' almost never means 'random' in a data pipeline -- it means the test is correctly detecting a real condition that itself occurs intermittently, and the job is to find what that condition correlates with, not to assume the test or the CI infrastructure is unreliable. The most common real cause behind an intermittent not_null/relationships failure on a fact table is a race condition between upstream data arrival and when the test runs: if this model depends on a source that's still being loaded by an upstream pipeline at the time dbt's CI job runs (timing varies run to run depending on exactly when the CI trigger fires relative to the source load's completion), the test will genuinely and correctly fail on some fraction of runs where it catches the source table mid-load, with a foreign key reference to a dimension row that hasn't landed yet or a column that's briefly null before a downstream correction step populates it.

To distinguish this from genuine data quality drift (as opposed to timing), I'd pull the actual failing rows from several different failed runs and compare them: if the failing rows are different each time and roughly correlate with 'most recently loaded' records specifically, that's strong evidence for a load-timing race rather than a structural data quality problem, since a structural issue would tend to recur on the same or a similar subset of rows. I'd also check whether CI is actually waiting on a real upstream completion signal (a proper dependency/trigger from the loading pipeline) or just running on a fixed schedule/webhook that happens to usually, but not always, land after the load finishes -- if it's the latter, that's close to a smoking gun.

The team's 're-run until green' habit is the more urgent problem to fix regardless of the root cause, because it actively destroys the only signal that would let anyone diagnose this properly, and it trains the team to treat test failures as noise rather than information -- by the time someone takes this seriously, the team has already built a habit of ignoring a specific class of failure, which is exactly the条件 under which a real data quality regression eventually ships to production undetected because it looked like 'just the usual flaky test.' The fix has two parts: immediately, add an explicit dependency/freshness check before this model runs (a source freshness test, or an actual pipeline-level dependency on the upstream load's completion signal rather than a fixed schedule), so the test only ever runs against data that's actually finished loading, which should make the failures either disappear (confirming the timing theory) or become consistently reproducible (meaning it really was a data issue, now unmasked). Structurally, I'd push for a team norm that any test failure gets investigated before a re-run, and that re-running without understanding why is explicitly called out as the anti-pattern it is -- a flaky-seeming test that turns out to be correctly catching a real intermittent problem is far more damaging once everyone's trained themselves to not look at it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first instinct with 'intermittent' is that it's probably not actually random -- it's probably a real condition that itself happens intermittently, and the job is to find the pattern, not write the test off as unreliable. For a not_null or relationships test on a fact table, the most common real cause I'd check first is a timing race with the upstream load -- if this model's source is still being populated by another pipeline when dbt's CI job happens to run, you'll get a genuine failure on whatever fraction of runs catch the source mid-load, with a reference to a dimension row that hasn't landed yet.

To tell that apart from a genuine data quality problem, I'd actually pull the failing rows from a handful of different failed runs and compare them. If it's different rows each time and they skew toward the most recently loaded records, that smells like a load-timing race, not a structural issue -- a real structural problem would tend to keep failing on the same kind of row. I'd also just check whether CI is actually waiting for a real signal that the upstream load finished, or just running on a schedule that happens to usually land after it -- if it's the latter, that's basically the answer right there.

But honestly, the thing I'd want to fix immediately, independent of root cause, is the team's habit of just re-running CI until it's green. That habit destroys the only signal that would ever let anyone actually diagnose this, and it trains everyone to treat a failing test as noise instead of information -- which is exactly how a real data quality regression eventually ships through unnoticed because it looked like 'the usual flaky thing.' So I'd add a real dependency check before this model runs, so the test only ever fires against data that's genuinely finished loading -- that should either make the failures disappear, which confirms the timing theory, or make them consistently reproducible, which means it actually was a real data problem the whole time. And I'd push hard on the team norm piece -- no re-running without at least glancing at why it failed first.
commonMistakes: Assuming an intermittent test failure means the test or CI infrastructure is unreliable rather than correctly detecting a real condition
Not pulling and comparing actual failing rows across multiple runs to distinguish timing issues from structural data quality issues
Allowing 're-run until green' to become a team habit, destroying the diagnostic signal
Not checking whether CI actually waits for a real upstream completion signal versus a fixed schedule
Fixing the symptom (making the test pass) rather than the actual race condition or data quality cause
keyPoints: Intermittent failures usually reflect a real, intermittently-occurring condition rather than test unreliability
A load-timing race with an upstream source is the most common cause of intermittent not_null/relationships failures
Comparing actual failing rows across runs distinguishes a timing race from genuine structural data quality drift
Re-running CI until green destroys the diagnostic signal and trains the team to ignore real failures
The durable fix adds an explicit upstream dependency/freshness check rather than relying on a fixed schedule

Correctly identifies a load-timing race as the likely root cause with a sound diagnostic method

questions.title: An ADF CI/CD Deployment That Works in Dev but Breaks in Production
questions.prompt: An Azure Data Factory ARM template deployment pipeline works perfectly in the dev environment but fails in production with a linked service authentication error, even though the pipeline definitions themselves are identical. Walk through the likely cause given this specific dev-vs-prod discrepancy, and the correct way to structure ARM template parameterization to prevent it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fact that the pipeline definitions are identical but the failure is specifically an authentication error on a linked service is the key clue: pipeline logic (activities, dependencies, control flow) is almost never what differs between environments in a well-structured ADF CI/CD setup -- what legitimately has to differ between dev and production is environment-specific configuration: connection strings, Key Vault references, authentication method, resource names. If that environment-specific configuration isn't properly externalized into ARM template parameters, the most common failure mode is exactly this one: the production deployment is accidentally deploying a linked service pointing at dev's Key Vault, dev's connection string, or dev's managed identity/service principal, because that value got baked into the ARM template as a literal rather than parameterized, and ADF's own 'publish' or the arm-template-parameters-definition.json generation didn't actually externalize that specific property.

The root mechanism in ADF's ARM-template-based deployment is the arm-template-parameters-definition.json file: ADF's template generation only turns a given linked service property into a deployable parameter if that property is explicitly listed in this definition file (or, for newer git-integrated setups, correctly marked for parameterization through the equivalent mechanism) -- properties not listed there get baked into the generated ARM template as the literal value they held in whichever environment generated the template (almost always dev, since that's usually where the ADF instance being actively developed and published from lives). If the specific authentication-related property on this linked service (a Key Vault URI, a specific secret name, an authentication type setting) isn't in that parameterization definition, every environment's deployment gets dev's literal value for it regardless of what parameter file values are supplied at deployment time for production -- which is exactly how production ends up silently trying to authenticate using dev's Key Vault/identity and failing.

The fix is to explicitly add the missing property to the arm-template-parameters-definition.json (or the modern equivalent parameterization configuration) so it actually becomes a deployable parameter, then supply the correct production value for that parameter in the production-specific parameters file used by the release pipeline (or via variable substitution in Azure DevOps/GitHub Actions release stages). Longer-term, the structural fix worth pushing for is a consistent convention -- every linked service's authentication-related properties (Key Vault references, connection strings, managed identity client IDs) should be parameterized by default as part of the team's ADF development standards, with a checklist or automated validation step in the CI pipeline that flags any linked service property that looks environment-specific but isn't present in the parameterization definition, so this class of bug gets caught before a production deployment rather than discovered by a production authentication failure.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Given the pipeline logic is identical and the failure is specifically an auth error on a linked service, I'm not looking at the pipelines at all -- I'm looking at what's supposed to differ between dev and prod but apparently isn't: connection details, Key Vault references, which identity is being used to authenticate. My first guess is that some property on this linked service got baked into the ARM template as a literal value from dev instead of being externalized as a parameter, so production is deploying with dev's actual connection info or dev's managed identity reference, and obviously failing to authenticate with it.

The mechanism behind that in ADF is the arm-template-parameters-definition.json file -- only properties explicitly listed there actually become real deployable parameters when the template gets generated. Anything not listed just gets hardcoded into the generated template using whatever value it had in the environment that generated it, which is almost always dev. So if the specific auth-related property here -- a Key Vault URI, a secret name, whatever -- isn't in that definition file, every environment gets dev's literal value no matter what you put in the production parameters file, because there's no parameter slot for it to land in.

The immediate fix is adding that missing property to the parameterization definition so it's actually a real parameter, then supplying the correct production value for it through the production parameters file in the release pipeline. The longer-term fix I'd push for is making this a standard checklist item -- every linked service's auth-related properties get parameterized by default as a team convention, and ideally there's an automated check in CI that flags anything that looks environment-specific sitting in a linked service but missing from the parameterization definition, so this gets caught in a PR review instead of as a production incident.
commonMistakes: Investigating pipeline logic differences when the pipelines are confirmed identical
Not knowing that arm-template-parameters-definition.json controls which properties actually become deployable parameters
Assuming all linked service properties are automatically parameterized by ADF's template generation
Fixing the immediate deployment without adding a check to catch the same class of bug for other linked services
Confusing a missing parameter value in the release pipeline with a missing parameter definition in the template generation
keyPoints: Pipeline logic is rarely what differs between environments; environment-specific configuration is
arm-template-parameters-definition.json controls which linked service properties actually become ARM template parameters
A property missing from that definition gets baked into the template as a literal value from whichever environment generated it
The fix adds the missing property to the parameterization definition and supplies the correct production value
A standing CI check or team convention should catch unparameterized environment-specific properties before deployment

Correctly explains the arm-template-parameters-definition.json mechanism
Proposes a correct immediate fix
Proposes a sound structural/preventive fix

questions.title: A Snowflake Data Sharing Consumer Seeing Stale Data After a Provider Refresh
questions.prompt: A downstream partner company consumes your Snowflake data share, and they report their dashboards are showing yesterday's numbers even though your provider-side table refreshed six hours ago. Your own provider-side queries against the shared table show current data. Walk through what's actually happening with Snowflake's secure data sharing in this scenario and where the staleness is most likely coming from.
questions.modelAnswer:
Snowflake's secure data sharing doesn't copy any data to the consumer account at all -- a share grants the consumer's account read access to reference the provider's actual underlying tables directly, metadata-only, with queries against the shared objects running against the live, current data in the provider's account at query time. That means the staleness almost certainly isn't happening inside Snowflake's sharing mechanism itself, since by design there's no separate stale copy for the sharing layer to be serving -- if the provider-side table is genuinely current, a consumer query run directly against the shared view/table through their own warehouse should see the same current data the provider sees, because it's the same physical data being queried, not a replica.

The most likely explanation, given this specific symptom, is one of three things sitting on the consumer's side of the boundary, not the sharing mechanism: first, and most common, the consumer may have materialized the shared data into their own table via a scheduled Task or a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT against the share, running on some schedule (nightly, say) -- if so, their 'dashboard' is querying their own materialized copy, not the live share, and that copy is only as fresh as their own refresh schedule, which has nothing to do with when the provider's underlying table last refreshed. Second, if the consumer is querying the share through a BI tool in import/extract mode (analogous to Power BI Import or a Tableau extract) rather than a live/DirectQuery-style connection, that tool's own extract refresh schedule, not the share's freshness, determines what the dashboard shows. Third, and worth ruling out directly, caching at either a result-cache layer on the consumer's warehouse or within whatever BI tool's own query/report cache could be serving a stale cached result rather than re-querying the share at all.

Confirming this means asking the consumer to run a direct, uncached SELECT with current timestamp comparisons straight against the shared object from a fresh Snowflake session (bypassing any BI tool or materialized intermediate table) -- if that direct query shows current data, the staleness is conclusively happening somewhere in the consumer's downstream pipeline (their materialization job, their BI extract schedule, or their cache), not in the share itself, and the fix is entirely on their side: either querying the share live instead of materializing it, or tightening whatever refresh schedule their materialization/extract process runs on. If that direct query against the share itself also shows stale data, that would be a genuinely unusual and much more serious finding worth escalating immediately, since it would mean the share's grant or the underlying table reference itself is somehow not pointing at current data, which contradicts how secure data sharing is designed to work and would warrant checking whether the correct, current version of the table is actually the one granted in the share.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd explain to the partner is how sharing actually works here, because it rules out most of the obvious suspects immediately -- Snowflake's secure data sharing doesn't copy any data anywhere. It just grants their account permission to query our actual live tables directly. There's no separate stale replica sitting in the sharing layer for this to be a bug in -- if our table is current, a live query against the share should see exactly that, because it's literally the same data.

So my money is on something happening on their side of the boundary, and there are really three usual suspects. Most common: they've probably got a scheduled job that materializes the shared data into their own table on some schedule, and their dashboard is actually querying that copy, not the live share -- so its freshness depends entirely on their refresh schedule, which has nothing to do with when our table last updated. Second possibility: if they're hitting the share through a BI tool in extract or import mode rather than a live connection, it's that tool's own extract refresh schedule driving what shows up, not the share itself. Third, worth just ruling out directly: some kind of result cache, either at their warehouse level or inside the BI tool, serving a stale cached result instead of actually re-querying.

To nail it down, I'd ask them to run a plain, uncached SELECT directly against the shared object from a fresh session, no BI tool, no intermediate table in the way. If that shows current data, it's conclusively something downstream on their end, and the fix is on them -- query the share live, or tighten whatever schedule their materialization or extract job runs on. If that direct query somehow still shows stale data, that would actually be a serious finding worth escalating immediately, because it would mean something's wrong with the share grant itself, which isn't how this is supposed to work at all.
commonMistakes: Assuming Snowflake data sharing replicates data to the consumer, making staleness a provider-side sharing bug
Not asking the consumer to test with a direct, uncached query against the share before assuming it's a provider issue
Overlooking BI tool extract/import mode as a source of staleness independent of the underlying data's freshness
Not considering a consumer-side materialization job as the most likely explanation
Escalating internally before ruling out the consumer-side causes first
keyPoints: Secure data sharing grants live, metadata-only access to the provider's actual tables, with no data copy
A query against a share should reflect current data unless something downstream is caching or materializing it
Consumer-side materialization jobs, BI extract schedules, or caching are the most likely sources of this staleness
A direct, uncached query against the share from the consumer isolates whether the issue is provider-side or consumer-side
True staleness in the share grant itself would be a rare, serious finding contradicting how sharing is designed to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that data sharing provides live access with no data copy
Correctly identifies consumer-side materialization/extract/caching as the likely cause
Describes a concrete diagnostic approach to isolate provider vs consumer side
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Databricks Job Failing Intermittently With No Clear Error Pattern
questions.prompt: A nightly Databricks job on an autoscaling cluster with spot instances fails roughly twice a week with a generic 'task failed' error, with no consistent stage or data volume pattern, while identical reruns usually succeed. Walk through how you'd distinguish a spot-instance eviction issue from an actual code/data bug, and what cluster configuration changes you'd consider versus what you'd explicitly avoid doing reflexively.
questions.modelAnswer:
The signature that points at spot eviction rather than a code/data bug is exactly what's described: non-reproducible failures with no consistent stage, no consistent data volume correlation, and -- critically -- the job usually succeeds on an identical rerun. A genuine code or data bug tends to be deterministic given the same input (the same bad row, the same edge case in a transformation, the same out-of-memory condition on the same oversized partition) and would therefore fail consistently, or at least correlate with something identifiable about the specific run (a particular day's data volume, a particular upstream source behaving differently); an infrastructure-level eviction is close to a Poisson process with respect to the job's own logic -- it can hit any stage, any executor, at any point, entirely independent of what the code is doing, which matches this symptom closely.

The direct confirmation is in the cluster event log and the Spark driver/executor logs for the failed runs specifically: Databricks surfaces spot instance eviction/reclamation events in the cluster's event log, and the Spark UI (even after the fact, if event logs are retained) shows executor loss events with a reason that, when it's a cloud-provider-initiated preemption, is distinguishable from an executor dying due to an out-of-memory error or a task throwing an application-level exception. Checking whether the failed runs specifically show an executor-lost-due-to-preemption event, correlated in time with the job's actual failure, is the concrete evidence needed before concluding this is an infrastructure issue rather than a latent bug.

Once confirmed as eviction-driven, the configuration response has to distinguish between resilience and root-cause elimination. Spark and Databricks have real mechanisms to tolerate spot eviction gracefully -- task-level retries (spark.task.maxFailures set above the default of 1, so a task lost to eviction gets automatically retried on a surviving executor rather than failing the whole job), and, more fundamentally, ensuring the job's critical path (especially the driver, and ideally a baseline of executors) isn't entirely spot-based -- a common and effective pattern is running the driver and a minimum fixed number of executors on on-demand instances while letting the autoscaling 'burst' capacity use spot, so losing spot capacity degrades throughput rather than failing the whole job outright. What I'd explicitly avoid doing reflexively is switching the entire cluster to on-demand instances as a blanket fix -- that does genuinely eliminate the eviction risk, but it also eliminates the cost savings spot instances exist to provide, and for a job that fails twice a week and otherwise succeeds on retry, a targeted fix (task retries plus a stable on-demand baseline) addresses the actual reliability need at a fraction of the cost increase of abandoning spot entirely. I'd also avoid the instinct to just add a blanket 'retry the whole job' wrapper at the orchestration level without first increasing task-level retry tolerance, since task-level retry recovers from an eviction mid-job far more cheaply than restarting the entire job from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The pattern itself is pretty telling -- no consistent stage, no consistent data volume correlation, and it usually just works on an identical rerun. A real code or data bug tends to be deterministic against the same input, so I'd expect it to fail the same way every time given the same data, or at least correlate with something specific about a given run. An infrastructure-level eviction doesn't care what the code is doing -- it can take out any executor at any stage at any time, which matches this symptom a lot better than a latent bug would.

To actually confirm it, I'd go check the cluster event log for the failed runs specifically -- Databricks logs spot eviction events there, and the Spark UI's executor-lost events usually distinguish a cloud-provider preemption from an executor dying because of an OOM or an actual application exception. If the failed runs show an executor lost to preemption right around when the job died, that's the confirmation.

Once I've got that, I'd think about this as two separate problems -- tolerating eviction gracefully versus eliminating it entirely, and those have very different costs. The resilience fix is bumping task-level retries above the default so a task lost to eviction just gets retried on a surviving executor instead of failing the whole job, and making sure the driver and some minimum baseline of executors are running on-demand rather than fully spot, so losing spot capacity slows things down instead of killing the job outright.

What I'd specifically avoid is reflexively switching the whole cluster to on-demand as the fix. That does eliminate the eviction risk, sure, but it also eliminates the entire reason spot instances were being used, and for something failing twice a week that otherwise succeeds on rerun, that's a disproportionate cost response to the actual problem. I'd also avoid just wrapping the whole job in an orchestration-level retry without first fixing task-level retry tolerance, because restarting the entire job from scratch is a much more expensive recovery than letting Spark retry just the one lost task.
commonMistakes: Treating a non-reproducible, success-on-rerun failure as a code bug worth debugging in the application logic
Not checking the cluster event log/Spark UI for actual eviction events before concluding root cause
Reflexively switching the entire cluster to on-demand instances, losing the cost benefit spot was providing
Wrapping the whole job in an orchestration-level retry instead of fixing task-level retry tolerance first
Assuming spark.task.maxFailures is already set above its restrictive default
keyPoints: Non-reproducible, stage-independent failures that usually succeed on rerun point at infrastructure, not code
Cluster event logs and Spark UI executor-lost events confirm spot eviction as the specific cause
Task-level retries (spark.task.maxFailures) let a job tolerate eviction without failing entirely
Running the driver and a baseline of executors on-demand limits the blast radius of spot eviction
Switching entirely to on-demand is a disproportionate fix that eliminates spot's cost benefit for an otherwise-tolerable failure rate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that the failure pattern points at infrastructure eviction, not a code/data bug
Describes a concrete method to confirm eviction via logs
Proposes sound resilience fixes (task retries, on-demand baseline)
Correctly identifies and avoids the disproportionate all-on-demand fix

questions.title: A Cross-Dialect Migration Bug: Silent Truncation After Moving From SQL Server to Snowflake
questions.prompt: After migrating a reporting database from SQL Server to Snowflake, a finance report's totals are subtly wrong for a small number of high-value transactions, but every migrated row count matches exactly between the two systems. Walk through the data type mapping issue most likely responsible for silent numeric truncation in a cross-dialect migration like this, and how you'd actually find it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Row counts matching exactly is actually a meaningful clue about where the bug isn't: this isn't a dropped-rows problem, every row made it across, which points specifically at a value-level transformation issue affecting a subset of rows rather than a load-completeness failure. Given that it's specifically high-value transactions that are wrong, the leading suspect in a SQL Server-to-Snowflake numeric migration is a precision/scale mismatch on a DECIMAL/NUMERIC column during the migration tooling's automatic type mapping -- if the migration tool (or a manually-written DDL translation) mapped SQL Server's DECIMAL(18,2) or similar to a Snowflake NUMBER with a narrower precision than the source actually used, or if an intermediate staging format (a CSV export/import step, or a tool that infers types rather than reading the source schema's declared precision) silently inferred a smaller precision from a sample of the data that happened not to include the largest values seen during sampling, every value that exceeds the narrower target precision either gets silently rounded, truncated, or in some tooling, raises an overflow error that got swallowed or converted to a NULL/default rather than failing the load loudly.

The second real possibility, also specific to high-value transactions, is a floating-point intermediate representation introduced somewhere in the migration pipeline -- if any step in the ETL/migration tool represents the value as a FLOAT/DOUBLE rather than preserving exact decimal arithmetic end to end (common in tools that use a generic intermediate type system, or in a naive CSV round-trip where a number gets parsed and reserialized through a floating-point-based language runtime), very large or very precise decimal values are exactly where floating-point representation error becomes visible, while smaller, rounder values would look fine by coincidence -- which matches 'wrong only for a small number of high-value transactions' precisely.

Finding it concretely: pull the source SQL Server values for a specific known-wrong transaction and compare them byte-for-byte/digit-for-digit against the Snowflake value for the same transaction ID, which immediately shows whether this is rounding, truncation, or a genuine floating-point artifact (a value like 1234567.895 becoming 1234567.89 is rounding/truncation; a value becoming something like 1234567.8949999999 is a floating-point artifact). Then check the actual DDL: compare the source column's exact declared precision/scale in SQL Server (via sys.columns/sys.types) against the target Snowflake column's declared NUMBER precision/scale, which directly confirms or rules out the precision-mismatch theory. If the DDL types match correctly on both sides, the next place to look is the migration tool's own intermediate representation/logs for this specific load -- whether it used a native connector that reads and preserves the source schema's exact type, versus a generic staging format that could have silently narrowed or floated the value in transit. The fix, once the specific mechanism is identified, is either correcting the target column's precision/scale to match or exceed the source's true maximum values (checking the full actual data distribution, not a sample, before deciding on a 'safe' target precision) or replacing whichever migration step introduced a floating-point intermediate with one that preserves exact decimal representation throughout.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that every row count matches tells me something useful right away -- this isn't a missing-data problem, it's a value-level problem affecting a subset of rows, since all the rows clearly made it across. Given it's specifically high-value transactions that are off, my first suspect is a precision and scale mismatch on whatever decimal or numeric column this is. If the migration tooling mapped the source's DECIMAL type to a narrower Snowflake NUMBER precision -- maybe because it inferred the target precision from a data sample that didn't happen to include the biggest values -- anything exceeding that narrower precision gets silently rounded or truncated, and depending on the tool, that might not even throw an error, just quietly produce a smaller number.

The other real possibility, and it fits the 'only high-value transactions' pattern just as well, is that something in the migration pipeline represented the value as a float at some intermediate step instead of preserving exact decimal arithmetic the whole way through. Floating-point error shows up exactly where you'd expect -- on large or oddly-precise values -- while smaller, rounder numbers happen to look fine by coincidence.

To actually find it, I'd grab one known-wrong transaction and compare the exact source value against the exact Snowflake value, digit for digit. If it's cleanly rounded or truncated, that points at precision mismatch. If it's got that telltale floating-point-artifact tail like .8949999999, that's a float conversion somewhere in the pipeline. Then I'd go check the actual DDL on both sides -- the source column's declared precision and scale versus the target NUMBER's declared precision and scale -- which tells me directly whether this is a schema mapping problem. If the DDL actually matches on both sides, I'd go look at whatever migration tool or staging step moved this data and check whether it used a connector that preserves the source's native type end to end, or some generic intermediate format that could have silently narrowed or floated the value along the way. Once I know which one it is, the fix is either correcting the target precision based on the real full data distribution, not a sample, or ripping out whatever step introduced the float conversion.
commonMistakes: Treating matching row counts as proof the migration is correct, without checking value-level accuracy
Assuming a data type mapping tool automatically preserves exact precision without verifying against the real data distribution
Not comparing exact source-vs-target values for a specific known-wrong record before theorizing about the cause
Overlooking floating-point intermediate representation as a cause distinct from precision/scale mismatch
Deciding on a 'safe' target precision based on a data sample rather than the full actual value distribution
keyPoints: Matching row counts rule out a completeness problem and point at a value-level transformation issue
A precision/scale mismatch on a decimal column is the leading suspect for silent truncation affecting only large values
A floating-point intermediate representation is a separate, equally plausible cause with a distinct signature
Comparing exact source-vs-target values for a specific transaction distinguishes rounding/truncation from floating-point artifacts
Comparing declared DDL precision/scale on both sides directly confirms or rules out the mapping theory

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons from matching row counts to a value-level, not completeness, issue
Correctly identifies precision/scale mismatch as the leading cause
Correctly identifies floating-point intermediate representation as an alternative cause
Describes a concrete, logical diagnostic sequence to confirm the exact mechanism

questions.title: Power BI Semantic Model Numbers Don't Reconcile With the Source Warehouse
questions.prompt: The finance team reports that a Power BI dashboard's monthly revenue figure is consistently about 3% higher than the number finance gets running the equivalent SQL directly against the Snowflake warehouse. The gap is consistent month over month, not random. Walk through how you'd systematically isolate where the discrepancy is coming from, given it's small, consistent, and not a wildly obvious bug.
questions.modelAnswer:
A small, consistent percentage gap -- not random, not wildly different -- is itself diagnostic: it rules out a gross logic error (that would typically produce a wildly different or wildly inconsistent number) and points at something systematic affecting a specific, bounded subset of the data or a specific aggregation step, applied consistently every month. The disciplined way to isolate it is to work from the bottom up rather than guessing at the DAX: first, confirm the semantic model's import or DirectQuery source query actually matches finance's SQL in scope -- row-level filters (does the Power BI model's source query or any applied RLS/model-level filter silently exclude or include a category of transactions, like test orders, refunds, or a specific transaction type, that finance's SQL does or doesn't include), and date boundary handling (an off-by-one on month boundaries, especially around time zone conversion if event timestamps are stored in UTC and 'month' is being evaluated inconsistently between the DAX measure's date logic and finance's SQL's date logic, is one of the most common sources of exactly this kind of small, consistent, every-month discrepancy).

Second, check for double-counting introduced by the model's relationships rather than its filters: if the fact table has a many-to-many or fan-out relationship to a dimension that isn't configured the way the measure's author assumed (for instance, a transaction legitimately joining to more than one row in a dimension table due to a data quality issue or a deliberate but unaccounted-for one-to-many relationship somewhere in the model), a simple SUM over that fact table can silently double-count a subset of rows -- and if that subset is a small, consistent fraction of transactions every month (say, transactions with multiple associated discount codes, or multi-line orders joined to a promotions table with more than one matching row), that produces exactly a small, consistent, every-month overstatement rather than a one-off anomaly.

Third, check the measure's actual aggregation logic against finance's SQL line by line for a specific month with enough granularity to spot a subtotal mismatch at the transaction or line-item level: run both calculations grouped by day instead of by month, which turns one discrepancy into thirty, each small, and makes any pattern (consistent on every day vs. concentrated on a few outlier days) immediately visible, and then drill into one specific day's discrepancy at the transaction level to directly identify which rows are being counted differently between the two paths. The specific finding in a case shaped exactly like this is very often one of: a fan-out relationship causing a small subset of rows to be double-counted, a date-boundary/time-zone mismatch shifting a handful of boundary transactions into or out of the reported month inconsistently between the two systems, or a filter exclusion (test data, voided transactions, a specific status code) applied in one path but not the other -- and the fix is whichever of these the day-level drill-down actually reveals, documented clearly enough that finance and the model can be reconciled with an explicit, named definition of what 'Revenue' includes and excludes in both places going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer:
A small, consistent percentage gap every single month is actually a useful signal, not just a vague 'something's wrong' -- it rules out a gross logic bug, since that would usually show up as wildly different or wildly inconsistent numbers, and it points at something systematic hitting a bounded subset of the data the same way every month.

I'd work bottom-up rather than guessing at the DAX. First I'd check scope -- does the Power BI model's source query or any applied filter, RLS included, include or exclude something finance's SQL handles differently, like test orders, refunds, or a specific transaction status. I'd also specifically check date boundary handling, because a UTC-versus-local-time month boundary mismatch between the DAX measure and finance's SQL is one of the most common causes of exactly this kind of small, every-month-consistent gap.

Second, I'd check for double counting from the model's relationships, not its filters. If the fact table fans out to a dimension in a way the measure's author didn't account for -- say, some transactions legitimately joining to more than one row in a promotions table -- a plain SUM over that fact table will quietly double count just those rows, and if that's a small, consistent fraction of transactions every month, that produces exactly this signature.

Third, I'd actually run both calculations at daily grain instead of monthly for one specific month, which turns one discrepancy into thirty smaller ones and makes it obvious whether it's spread evenly or concentrated on specific days. Then I'd drill into one day's gap down to the transaction level and literally compare which rows are counted on each side. In my experience a gap shaped exactly like this usually turns out to be one of three things: a fan-out double-count, a date-boundary mismatch, or a filter exclusion applied in one path but not the other -- and whichever one the daily drill-down actually reveals is the one I'd fix, and then I'd make sure finance and the model end up with an explicit, written-down, agreed definition of what counts as Revenue in both places so this doesn't quietly drift apart again.
questions.example: Drilling to daily grain reveals the gap concentrates on the last day of each month: transactions timestamped in UTC near midnight are being bucketed into the next month by the DAX measure's date logic while finance's SQL converts to local time first -- a handful of boundary transactions shifting months every month, producing the same small, consistent monthly overstatement.
commonMistakes: Assuming a small, consistent gap must be a minor rounding issue rather than investigating systematically
Jumping straight into rewriting the DAX measure before confirming scope (filters/RLS) matches finance's SQL
Not checking for fan-out/double-counting relationships as a cause distinct from filter mismatches
Comparing only at monthly grain instead of drilling to daily or transaction-level detail to localize the discrepancy
Fixing the number without documenting an explicit, shared definition of the metric to prevent future drift
keyPoints: A small, consistent percentage gap points at a systematic, bounded cause, not a gross logic error
Scope mismatches (filters, RLS, date boundary/time zone handling) are a leading candidate
Fan-out relationships causing silent double-counting are a separate, equally plausible candidate
Drilling from monthly to daily to transaction-level grain isolates exactly where the two calculations diverge
The fix should include a documented, shared metric definition to prevent future reconciliation drift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that a small, consistent gap points at a systematic, bounded cause
Correctly identifies filter/scope and date-boundary mismatches as leading candidates
Correctly identifies fan-out/double-counting as a distinct candidate
Describes a concrete drill-down methodology to isolate the cause

questions.title: Choosing Between Fabric, Databricks, and Snowflake for a Mid-Size Retailer's Modern Platform
questions.prompt: A mid-size retailer currently runs Power BI on top of an aging on-prem SQL Server warehouse and wants to modernize onto a cloud lakehouse/warehouse platform. The team is a mix of strong Power BI/DAX skills, moderate SQL skills, and no existing Spark or Python expertise. They have heavy existing Microsoft 365/Azure AD investment, a need for both BI dashboards and a future data science initiative, and a cost-conscious leadership team. Walk through how you'd actually evaluate Microsoft Fabric, Databricks, and Snowflake for this specific organization, not in the abstract, and make a recommendation with explicit trade-offs.
questions.modelAnswer:
The honest starting point is that all three platforms can technically serve this retailer's stated needs -- this isn't a capability gap decision, it's a fit decision shaped by the team's existing skills, the existing ecosystem investment, and the cost profile of the actual workload, and treating it as 'which platform is objectively best' rather than 'which platform is the best fit for this team and this moment' is the most common mistake in this kind of evaluation.

Fabric's case here is strong on fit: the team already has deep Power BI/DAX skill and heavy Azure AD/M365 investment, and Fabric is specifically designed to extend that investment -- the same workspace and governance model, Direct Lake letting existing Power BI skills get large-model performance without learning a new query engine, and OneLake's single-copy-of-data design reducing the duplication cost between a warehouse layer and a BI layer that would otherwise exist. The capacity-based (CU) pricing model is also easier for a cost-conscious leadership team to reason about as a single predictable line item than Snowflake's or Databricks' consumption-based billing, at least initially. The risk is that Fabric is the newest of the three in market maturity for the heavier data engineering and future data science work the retailer is anticipating -- the Spark/notebook experience and the broader third-party tooling ecosystem are less battle-tested than Databricks', and capacity-based pricing can become a real bottleneck requiring careful workload scheduling once concurrent BI and engineering workloads start competing for the same CU pool, which this team has no existing experience managing.

Databricks' case is strongest for the future data science initiative specifically -- it's the most mature environment here for Spark, MLflow, and a genuine notebook-first data science workflow, and Unity Catalog's governance model is the most battle-tested of the three for a lakehouse that needs to serve both BI and ML consumers well. The real cost against this team specifically is the skills gap: a team with no existing Spark or Python expertise is going to face a real ramp-up curve, and Databricks' BI story, while real via Power BI connectors and SQL warehouses, is less of a first-class, native experience for the team's existing Power BI muscle than Fabric's Direct Lake integration is -- this isn't Databricks being worse at BI, it's that the team's specific skill investment pays off less immediately there.

Snowflake's case is strongest on SQL-centric simplicity and proven multi-cloud flexibility -- a moderate-SQL-skill team can be productive quickly, its warehouse elasticity and per-second billing are well understood and well documented for cost control, and Snowpark/Cortex give a real, if less mature than Databricks', path into the data science initiative without leaving the platform. The case against it here is that it doesn't naturally extend the existing Azure/M365 investment the way Fabric does -- it's platform-agnostic by design, which is a genuine strength in general but means this team would be adding a net-new vendor relationship and a net-new governance/identity integration layer on top of an organization that's already heavily invested in the Microsoft ecosystem, rather than extending something they already have.

Given everything stated -- strong Power BI skills, moderate SQL, no Spark/Python, heavy Azure investment, cost-consciousness, and a future (not immediate) data science need -- I'd recommend Fabric as the primary platform, specifically because it's the option that converts the team's existing skill investment into immediate productivity and extends rather than duplicates the existing Azure/M365 governance surface, while being explicit with leadership about the trade-off: Fabric's data engineering and data science tooling is the least mature of the three right now, so the data science initiative should be scoped with that maturity gap explicitly acknowledged, revisited in 12-18 months as Fabric's roadmap matures, rather than assuming it will be as capable as a dedicated Databricks environment on day one.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd push back gently on 'which platform is best' as the framing, because all three can technically do what this retailer needs -- this is a fit question, not a capability gap, and it's shaped heavily by what this specific team already knows and what they're already invested in.

Fabric's strongest argument here is that it doesn't ask this team to learn anything new to get value immediately -- they've already got strong Power BI and DAX skills, and Fabric's Direct Lake and workspace model let that skill translate directly into performance on a much bigger lakehouse without anyone learning Spark first. It also extends their existing Azure AD and M365 investment instead of adding a new one, and capacity-based pricing is genuinely easier for a cost-conscious leadership team to reason about as one predictable number. Where I'd be honest about the risk: Fabric is the newest of the three for serious data engineering and the data science work they're planning down the road, and capacity contention between BI and engineering workloads on one CU pool is a real operational thing this team has zero experience managing yet.

Databricks is genuinely the strongest option for that future data science initiative specifically -- most mature Spark and MLflow environment of the three, most battle-tested governance for mixed BI-plus-ML consumers. But this team has no Spark or Python background at all, so there's a real ramp-up cost, and while Databricks can absolutely serve BI well, it's not going to feel as immediately native to this team's existing Power BI instincts as Fabric does.

Snowflake is the simplest story for a moderate-SQL team to get productive fast, with well-understood, well-documented cost controls and a real, if less mature, data science path through Snowpark and Cortex. The honest downside for this specific org is that it doesn't extend anything they already have -- it's a net-new vendor and a net-new identity/governance integration on top of an organization that's already deeply invested in Azure.

Given everything about this team specifically, I'd recommend Fabric, and I'd be upfront with leadership about the trade-off I'm making on their behalf: we're prioritizing immediate productivity and extending existing investment over picking the most mature data engineering platform, and the data science initiative needs to be scoped knowing Fabric's tooling there is still catching up, with an explicit plan to revisit that assumption in a year or so as the platform matures.

deepDive.heading: What would change the recommendation
deepDive.content: If the data science initiative were an immediate, not future, requirement with a hard deadline, I'd flip toward Databricks despite the skills gap, because a maturity gap on day one is a harder problem to paper over than a learning curve the team has 12-18 months to climb. If the organization had any meaningful non-Azure cloud footprint or multi-cloud requirement (an AWS or GCP presence for a different business unit), that would push toward Snowflake's platform-agnostic design regardless of the Power BI skill advantage Fabric offers, since platform lock-in risk would outweigh the short-term productivity gain.

deepDive.heading: The capacity-planning risk I'd flag explicitly to leadership
deepDive.content: Fabric's CU-based pricing is easy to reason about as a single number until BI refreshes and data engineering workloads start competing for the same capacity pool, which is exactly the kind of contention this team has no operational experience diagnosing yet. I'd budget for either a second, smaller capacity to isolate workloads early, or an explicit plan to monitor the Fabric Capacity Metrics app from day one rather than treating capacity sizing as a one-time decision made at purchase.

commonMistakes: Evaluating platforms purely on feature checklists rather than fit with the team's existing skills and ecosystem investment
Assuming the newest platform's maturity gaps don't matter if the need is only 'future,' without an explicit revisit plan
Treating Snowflake's platform-agnosticism as a universal advantage rather than weighing it against existing ecosystem investment
Underestimating the ramp-up cost of a Spark/Python-centric platform for a team with no existing experience in either
Making a platform recommendation without being explicit about what evidence would change it
keyPoints: All three platforms are technically capable; the decision is about fit with team skills, ecosystem investment, and cost model
Fabric's advantage is directly extending existing Power BI/DAX skill and Azure/M365 investment
Databricks is the strongest fit for the future data science initiative but carries the largest skills ramp-up
Snowflake offers SQL-centric simplicity and multi-cloud flexibility at the cost of not extending existing Azure investment
A sound recommendation states explicit trade-offs and what would change the decision, not just a conclusion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Evaluates all three platforms against the organization's actual stated constraints, not generic feature comparison
Makes a clear recommendation with sound justification tied to the team's skills and ecosystem
Explicitly states trade-offs and risks of the chosen platform
Identifies what would change the recommendation

questions.title: Lambda vs. Kappa Architecture for a Real-Time Inventory Platform
questions.prompt: A retailer needs both near-real-time inventory counts on the store floor (seconds of latency) and accurate, auditable daily/monthly inventory reconciliation for finance. Compare Lambda and Kappa architecture for this specific case, explain the real reason Lambda architecture historically exists (not just 'it has two paths'), and make a concrete recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lambda architecture's real justification historically wasn't 'two paths for redundancy' -- it emerged because stream processing engines, for a long time, genuinely couldn't be trusted to correctly handle the full complexity of accurate, exactly-once, fully-correct computation over unbounded data at the volumes some organizations needed, especially anything involving complex joins, late data, or reprocessing historical corrections. The batch layer existed because batch processing frameworks were mature and well-understood for producing a provably correct, reprocessable answer over a complete, bounded dataset, while the speed layer existed purely to cover the latency gap until the batch layer's next run caught up -- the serving layer then merged the two, typically overwriting the speed layer's approximate recent view with the batch layer's authoritative one once it became available. The cost of that design was real and persistent: maintaining two separate codebases implementing the same business logic (one in a streaming framework, one in a batch framework), which is a long-term source of exactly the kind of logic drift and reconciliation bugs covered elsewhere in this stack -- two independently-written definitions of the same computation inevitably disagree eventually.

Kappa architecture's premise is that modern stream processing engines (Spark Structured Streaming, Flink) have matured enough to handle both the real-time and the 'eventually correct, reprocessable' requirements through one single pipeline and one single codebase, by treating the event log itself (Kafka, or Delta as an append-and-replay-capable log) as the system of record and allowing full reprocessing from that log when correctness needs to be recomputed, rather than maintaining a structurally separate batch path. For this inventory scenario specifically, Kappa is well-justified for the fast-moving inventory-count side: Structured Streaming with watermarking can give the store floor near-real-time counts while still handling a bounded amount of late-arriving correction data through the same single pipeline, and if a bug or a late correction requires recomputing history, replaying the Kafka/Delta log through the same stream processing logic (rather than maintaining a separate batch job doing the same math differently) is both operationally simpler and structurally immune to the two-codebase-drift problem Lambda is prone to.

The case for still keeping something structurally closer to a batch-style reconciliation step -- not necessarily full Lambda, but not pure unqualified Kappa either -- comes specifically from finance's requirement: an auditable, point-in-time-correct monthly reconciliation isn't really a 'faster vs. slower view of the same computation' problem, which is what Kappa is built to unify; it's a fundamentally different correctness requirement, closer to 'produce a figure that can be defended against an audit, incorporating every correction received by a hard close date, with an immutable record of exactly what was known at the time of close.' Even a mature Kappa pipeline benefits from an explicit, scheduled reconciliation job -- running the same underlying stream-processing logic in batch/replay mode against the full log up to the close cutoff, rather than trusting the continuously-running streaming aggregation's live state to double as the audited number -- specifically because finance needs a deliberately-triggered, reproducible, timestamped computation they can point to, not a live number that kept changing as late corrections arrived after the fact.

My recommendation: build this as a Kappa-style single pipeline for the real-time inventory-count use case (one codebase, Kafka/Delta as the replayable log, Structured Streaming with an appropriately-bounded watermark), but add a deliberate, explicitly-scheduled, batch-triggered reconciliation run of that same pipeline's logic against the full log as of each month's close -- which isn't Lambda's dual-codebase problem, since it's the same logic executed in a different mode/trigger, but gives finance the explicit, auditable, point-in-time artifact their requirement actually needs. This gets the store floor real-time counts without maintaining two independently-written definitions of 'inventory count,' and gives finance something more defensible than 'whatever the live aggregation happened to say at month-end.'
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by being precise about why Lambda architecture exists in the first place, because the usual explanation -- 'two paths, one fast one correct' -- undersells the real reason. It existed because stream processing engines, for a long time, genuinely weren't trustworthy enough to handle complex, exactly-once, fully correct computation over unbounded data on their own, especially with joins or late corrections. So you kept a batch layer around specifically because batch processing was the mature, provably-correct option, and the speed layer was just there to cover the latency gap until batch caught up. The real cost of that setup is maintaining two separate codebases computing the same business logic, which inevitably drift apart over time -- that's the actual tax Lambda charges, not just operational complexity.

Kappa's bet is that modern streaming engines have gotten good enough that you don't need that second codebase anymore -- you treat the event log itself as the source of truth, and if you ever need to recompute history correctly, you replay the log through the same single pipeline rather than maintaining a separate batch job doing the same math a different way. For the store-floor inventory counts here, that's a strong fit -- Structured Streaming with a sensible watermark gets near-real-time counts, and if something needs recomputing, replaying the log through that same logic is both simpler and doesn't carry Lambda's drift risk.

Where I wouldn't go full unqualified Kappa is finance's reconciliation requirement, and that's not really about speed versus correctness at all -- it's a fundamentally different kind of correctness. Finance doesn't want 'the fastest available view of the number,' they want a defensible, auditable figure that reflects every correction received by a hard close date, with a record of exactly what was known at that moment. Even with a solid Kappa pipeline, I'd still run an explicit, scheduled reconciliation pass -- same underlying logic, run in a deliberate batch/replay mode against the full log as of the close cutoff -- rather than just trusting whatever the live streaming aggregation's current state happens to say. That's not Lambda's two-codebase problem, since it's the same logic just triggered differently, but it gives finance the explicit, reproducible artifact their requirement actually needs.

So my recommendation is Kappa for the real-time path, with a deliberately-scheduled reconciliation run of that same pipeline logic for finance's close -- one codebase doing double duty in two different trigger modes, rather than two codebases that'll eventually disagree with each other.

deepDive.heading: Why this isn't secretly Lambda architecture again
deepDive.content: The distinction that matters is whether the batch/reconciliation path is an independently-written implementation of the business logic, or the exact same pipeline logic triggered differently against the same log. Lambda's real cost is two codebases drifting apart; running the same Structured Streaming transformation logic in a scheduled batch/replay invocation against the full Kafka/Delta history as of a cutoff doesn't introduce that risk, because there's still only one implementation of 'how to compute inventory count' -- only the trigger and the time window being processed differ.

deepDive.heading: Where this design would actually break down
deepDive.content: If the finance reconciliation logic genuinely needed business rules that differ from the real-time inventory count (e.g., adjustments, write-offs, or manual corrections that only apply at month-end and never to the live store-floor number), then it stops being 'the same logic in a different mode' and becomes a real second definition -- at that point, accepting a second, explicitly-named reconciliation-specific logic layer (not hiding it inside the same pipeline) is more honest than forcing an artificial unification, and the Lambda-style cost of maintaining two definitions has to be explicitly accepted and documented, not architected away by pretending it's unified when it isn't.

commonMistakes: Describing Lambda architecture as just 'two paths for redundancy' without explaining the historical correctness-limitation reason it existed
Assuming Kappa architecture eliminates the need for any reconciliation step just because stream processing has matured
Treating finance's reconciliation requirement as a speed-vs-correctness trade-off rather than a fundamentally different correctness requirement (auditability)
Building a second, independently-written reconciliation codebase without recognizing that reintroduces Lambda's drift risk
Not distinguishing 'same logic run in a different mode' from 'a genuinely different set of business rules' when designing the reconciliation path
keyPoints: Lambda architecture historically exists because stream processing couldn't be trusted for full correctness over unbounded data, not just for redundancy
Lambda's real ongoing cost is two independently-written codebases implementing the same logic, which drift apart
Kappa unifies real-time and reprocessable correctness into one pipeline by treating the log as replayable source of truth
Finance's auditability requirement is a different correctness need than real-time speed, best served by a scheduled replay of the same logic, not a second codebase
The recommendation should distinguish same-logic-different-trigger from a genuinely separate set of business rules

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the historical, correctness-driven justification for Lambda architecture
Correctly explains Kappa's premise and fit for the real-time inventory use case
Correctly reasons about finance's requirement as a distinct correctness need, not a speed trade-off
Makes a clear, well-justified architectural recommendation

questions.title: Deciding Where to Fix a Broken Upstream Field in a Medallion Architecture
questions.prompt: A source system's customer_phone field occasionally arrives malformed (missing country codes, inconsistent formatting, some values that are clearly test data like '555-555-5555') in a medallion-architecture lakehouse. Three engineers propose fixing it in three different layers: one wants to fix it in bronze during ingestion, one wants to fix it in silver, one wants to leave raw data alone everywhere and fix it only in a gold-layer view. Walk through the actual design principle that should decide this, not just pick a favorite.
questions.modelAnswer:
The principle that should decide this isn't a preference, it's what each layer is actually for: bronze exists specifically to preserve an unmodified, replayable record of exactly what the source system sent, which is the entire reason bronze has value as a layer at all -- if you clean or alter data on the way into bronze, you've permanently destroyed the ability to ever ask 'what did the source actually send us, bugs and all,' which matters enormously the first time you need to debug a source-system issue, prove to an auditor what was received, or discover that your cleaning logic itself had a bug and now has no ground truth to compare against. Fixing it in bronze is the one option that should be ruled out immediately regardless of which specific cleaning logic is proposed, because it conflates ingestion with transformation and permanently forecloses the ability to reprocess history if the cleaning rules themselves turn out to be wrong.

The real decision is between silver and gold, and that comes down to whether the cleaning logic is a widely-reusable, stable business rule or a presentation-specific, consumer-specific transformation. Silver's job is to apply conformance and quality rules that make data trustworthy and usable across multiple downstream consumers -- deduplication, standard type casting, and crucially, data quality rules that represent a genuine, durable business judgment about what 'valid' means (a phone number needs a country code to be usable for SMS marketing; '555-555-5555' and other obviously-synthetic patterns are known test data that should never reach a customer-facing system). If the phone number cleaning logic is exactly this kind of durable, reusable rule -- true for every consumer of this field, not just one dashboard's specific need -- it belongs in silver, applied once, so every downstream consumer (gold tables, ML features, operational exports) inherits the same clean definition rather than each one re-implementing (and potentially subtly disagreeing on) phone number validation independently.

Gold-layer, consumer-specific views are the right place only for transformations that are genuinely specific to one business consumption pattern rather than universally true -- formatting a phone number for display in a specific regional format for one specific report, for instance, is a legitimate gold-layer concern, but 'is this a real, usable phone number at all' is not a presentation preference, it's a fact about the data that every consumer needs the same answer to. Pushing a universal data quality rule all the way to gold means every gold table and every downstream consumer either has to reimplement the same validation logic or risks disagreeing with another gold table that implements it slightly differently -- which is exactly the kind of metric/definition drift that causes reconciliation problems between reports later.

The actual architectural answer: bronze stays untouched (preserve the real, possibly-malformed source record, with its own ingestion timestamp and lineage, forever replayable); silver applies the durable, reusable business rule -- standardizing format, adding country codes where inferable, and flagging (not necessarily deleting) known-test-data patterns with an explicit is_valid_phone or similar quality flag rather than silently dropping the raw value, so the judgment is visible and auditable rather than hidden; gold then consumes the already-validated silver data and applies only genuinely presentation-specific logic on top. This also means when (not if) the cleaning rule itself needs to change, there's exactly one place to change it, and bronze's untouched history means reprocessing silver under the corrected rule is always possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd settle this by going back to what each layer is actually for, not by picking a favorite among the three engineers. Bronze exists to preserve exactly what the source sent, unmodified -- that's its entire value. The moment you clean data on the way into bronze, you've permanently lost the ability to ever ask 'what did the source system actually send us,' which you will want the first time you're debugging an upstream issue or discovering your own cleaning logic had a bug and has nothing to compare against. So fixing it in bronze is off the table immediately, no matter how reasonable the specific cleaning rule sounds.

The real question is silver versus gold, and that comes down to one thing: is this a durable, reusable business rule that's true for every consumer, or is it specific to how one report wants to present the data. 'A valid phone number needs a country code, and 555-555-5555 is known test data that should never reach anything customer-facing' -- that's not a presentation choice, that's a fact about the data that every single downstream consumer needs the same answer to. That belongs in silver, applied once, so every gold table, every ML feature, every export inherits the identical definition instead of five different teams reimplementing phone validation slightly differently and eventually disagreeing with each other.

Gold-layer, consumer-specific transformations are the right call for something that's genuinely only true for one specific use -- formatting a number for display in a specific regional style for one particular report, sure, that's a gold concern. But 'is this real data at all' isn't a formatting preference, and pushing it all the way to gold just means every gold table has to either redo that validation or risk getting it wrong differently than the table next to it.

So the actual answer: leave bronze completely alone, apply this specific rule once in silver -- standardize the format, add country codes where it's inferable, and flag known-test-data patterns explicitly with something like an is_valid_phone column rather than silently deleting the raw value, so the judgment is visible rather than hidden -- and let gold build on top of already-validated data, only adding whatever's genuinely specific to one consumption pattern. And when this rule inevitably needs to change later, there's exactly one place to go fix it, and bronze's untouched history means we can always reprocess silver under the new rule.
commonMistakes: Cleaning or transforming data during bronze ingestion, destroying the ability to debug or reprocess from true source state
Treating a universal data quality rule as a gold-layer presentation concern, causing it to be reimplemented inconsistently across gold tables
Silently dropping or nulling malformed values instead of flagging them, losing a real data quality signal
Not distinguishing 'durable business rule true for every consumer' from 'presentation-specific transformation for one consumer' when deciding the layer
Assuming the layer decision is a matter of team preference rather than a structural principle tied to each layer's purpose
keyPoints: Bronze must remain unmodified to preserve replayability and true source-of-truth debugging capability
The silver-vs-gold decision hinges on whether the rule is a durable, universal business rule or a consumer-specific presentation choice
Universal data quality rules belong in silver, applied once, so every downstream consumer inherits a consistent definition
Flagging malformed data explicitly, rather than silently dropping it, preserves a useful data quality signal
Bronze's untouched history enables safe reprocessing of silver whenever the cleaning rule itself needs correction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rules out cleaning data at bronze ingestion with sound justification
Correctly articulates the silver-vs-gold decision principle (durable rule vs. presentation-specific)
Proposes flagging rather than silently dropping malformed data
Clear, accurate overall explanation with a concrete recommendation

questions.title: Designing Unity Catalog Governance Across Three Business Units With Different Compliance Needs
